items.text:
Things to know if you get cancer (2026 Edition)

2026.10.14

I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far.

You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation.

AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note.

You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups.

You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines. You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case.

If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is.

Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion.

I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time.

Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation. Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors.

Note, since this is on the front page of Hacker News right now. exhilaration suggested that if you are within a 2-3 hour drive of a major cancer center, go there instead of your local community hospital. Use the US News cancer hospital rankings. The top centers usually take your insurance, so use vacation days and book a hotel if you have to. The largest benefit I saw was speed. At MD Anderson I got a question answered within 20 minutes of a visit, because the doctor called the pathologist who he was on a first name basis with. If that wasn’t at a cancer center, it would have taken days, or more likely the question never would have been answered at all (I had asked my oncologist about this and he’d just shrugged). The rest of the HN comments are worth reading too.

items.title: How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet
items.author: sighborg

items.text:
Not-Ship turns one next week!! To mark it, I'll be kicking off a campaign for new members. I won't spam you; free subscribers will only get three extra emails on top of the weekly edition.

But first, can I ask for a small birthday present? Hit reply and finish this: I read Not-Ship because...

💙 Amanda

Support Not-Ship!

Last week I wrote about how Amazon's search page is designed to screw you over: the top row trap, the swamp of ads, the discount-washing. Today, I'll explain what's going on behind the scenes, and how Amazon's rules make sure prices stay high not just at Amazon, but everywhere you shop.

In a nutshell, here's what's happening:

This isn't just my theory. This system is at the heart of the US Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) upcoming antitrust case against Amazon.

Let's get into it.

Amazon charges sellers a lot of fees

Amazon relies on independent sellers to populate its online marketplace, and it charges them to be on the site. Amazon takes a big cut. In 2014, this was about 19% of sales. But today, many sellers hand close to half of every sale to Amazon. Half!

Amazon's basic commission (15% of the sale price in most categories) is in line with what eBay and Walmart charge. What pushes Amazon's cut higher are the other fees stacked on top.

Where an Amazon sale goes

Based on an apparel seller that opts for Amazon fulfillment, storage, returns and advertising.

There's the referral fee, which is the commission Amazon takes on every sale. The fulfillment fee is the cost to have Amazon pack and ship items from its warehouses. Then there's advertising: those sponsored spots in the top row we saw in last week's article.

Of these costs, only the referral fee is mandatory. Sellers can choose to ship orders themselves, for example, or forgo advertising. But in practice, the choice isn't actually much of a choice.

Here's what it looks like for a seller considering these so-called options:

In other words, the real choice for sellers isn't between paying for extras or not; it's between making sales or not. The FTC calls Prime eligibility, which effectively requires Amazon's fulfillment service, "a virtual necessity for doing business on Amazon." It says the same of advertising.

So, sellers have to raise prices

Here's where the fees are passed on to us consumers. When sellers give roughly half of their sales to Amazon, the other half isn't profit. That money has to cover making the product, shipping it to Amazon's warehouses, paying staff and everything else. So even if they wanted to absorb Amazon's fees on your behalf, most companies can't afford to. They have to raise their prices.

Don't forget, Amazon's biggest single fee — the referral fee — is a percentage of the price. So when prices go up, Amazon's cut goes up, too.

And they can't charge less elsewhere

Now here's where it gets really crazy. Amazon's Fair Pricing Policy lets it remove the Buy Box (the "Add to Cart" button), or even suspend a seller, if they're offering their item cheaper elsewhere. So, a seller who raises prices on Amazon to cover the fees has to raise them everywhere else too — even on their own website! — or risk losing their Amazon sales.

The consequence is clear: We pay Amazon prices, even when we're not shopping on Amazon.

It's been documented again and again. In 2024, Amazon sellers told CNBC they lost the Buy Box after Target put their products on sale. In an ongoing lawsuit, California's attorney general alleges Amazon pushed brands to get Walmart, Target and other retailers to raise their prices. And when progressive media outlet More Perfect Union reported on this, they even found an Amazon seller who was suspended over a one-cent price gap with Target.

Ideally, market competition would sort this out. High prices send shoppers elsewhere and force fees down. But when sellers can't charge less anywhere else, there's nowhere cheaper to go.

There's no easy way out

For sellers, this is frustrating. So, why don't they just leave? Because Amazon is where the shoppers are: it accounts for about 40% of all US online retail sales. For many sellers, not being on Amazon isn't an option.

At least regulators have noticed. In 2023, the FTC and 17 US states sued Amazon, arguing that it illegally maintains its monopoly power by, among other things, punishing sellers who offer lower prices elsewhere, effectively forcing them to use its warehouses and charging ever-higher fees. Amazon denies any wrongdoing, and the case is set to go to trial next year. In Europe, Germany ordered Amazon to stop controlling its sellers' prices earlier this year, though the decision isn't yet final.

After last week's piece, a Not-Ship reader wrote to say none of this is new: plenty of online stores push ads and fake discounts. That is true. But what's different about Amazon is its reach. When prices increase on Amazon, they tend to increase elsewhere too. You can, of course, choose not to shop on Amazon. But if the FTC is right, you may be paying Amazon's prices anyway.

FULL DISCLOSURE

I spent two years working at the Washington Post, which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos owns. During that time, he was busy dismantling the publication, so he wasn't well loved in the newsroom.

CLASSIC ENSHITTIFICATION

In August, I saw Cory Doctorow speak at the Edinburgh International Book Festival. His enshittification concept — the process by which online platforms shift from serving their users to squeezing them — inspired this two-part series on Amazon. If you want to understand it all a lot better, I highly recommend his book Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It. Somehow it makes antitrust issues both accessible and entertaining!

FROM ELSEWHERE

Here's what I found interesting, important or delightful this week:

Life after death? Alvin Chang's latest masterpiece has dropped! It’s about what people around the world believe happens after we die, drawn from surveys of nearly 130,000 people in 23 countries. (Proud to count Alvin as a Not-Ship subscriber 💙.)

Stunning embroidery. If you haven't seen the work of Irene Saputra, get yourself over to Instagram. Endlessly inspirational.

Instant knowledge. The Ars Notoria was a medieval magic book that promised scholars university learning through prayers, rituals and diagrams. No studying required!

MORE NOT-SHIP

In annual reports, fossil fuel companies have a new playbook for greenwashing

Words are cheap — especially when they’re about the future.

What’s good for Amazon is good for ... Amazon

How the world’s largest company makes you pay more for less.

Birds might help us get through this

The mental health benefits of “joy watching” are what we need right now.

items.title: Do dentists know what they're doing?
items.author: doitLP
items.summary:
I’m 17 and my jaw has been hurting, right at the hinge on the right side.

My mom has crowded teeth. My dad has gaps. I must have gotten a little of both
items.text:
I’m 17 and my jaw has been hurting, right at the hinge on the right side.

My mom has crowded teeth. My dad has gaps. I must have gotten a little of both because my teeth are straight and even. Good thing, because I’m in high school and braces would dissolve what small nuggets of game I have.

‘Well!’ declares the dentist as he emerges from my mouth. He pulls off his glove and I close my jaw. There’s a pop that could have come from either.

‘The thing is that the two halves of your face didn’t grow at the same rate. Here, take a look.’ He holds up a mirror and I see my disfiguration for the first time. The right side of my jaw is a little crooked. My nose on that side is angled, my eyelid is a slightly different shape.

‘Oh wow…’

I am shocked and embarrassed. I touch my face. I had no idea.

‘So, do I need braces?’

‘No, but your bite is a bit off. Fractions of a millimeter here and there.’ His own teeth strobe out from between his lips as he talks. They rival the overhead lamp for xenon brilliance, accentuated by his deeply tanned skin.

‘You’ll want to get it corrected or you could end up wearing your teeth down. I can do it today if you’re up for it?’

‘I’m not sure…what about my jaw?’

‘Oh it will make that better actually. Your jaw will slot right into place after this. No more sliding around to find the right bite.’

‘Are you sure? Because I really don’t—’

‘If you were my son, I would say the same thing.’

‘OK,’ I say, ‘Let’s do it.’

Tooth reshaping was a euphemism. Voluntary torture would have been more accurate. My teeth fit together better alright. But they are shorter now, and that makes the impingement of my jaw into the right socket worse.

Fucking guy. Never going there again. That hygienist was pretty though…mom-pretty, but still.

I wish I had never done it. But hey, at least I didn’t have to get braces.

I’m 20, in Florida. My face is still warm from the radiation bath the ancient x-ray machine gave me. It is a tall, forbidding machine that would have at least a dozen skulls painted on its nose cone if it was a fighter plane. The office is a couple rooms in an office building basement. The hygienist is out for a back surgery and the front desk lady is sick. So the sweaty old dentist is doing it all himself today.

‘Well no cavities,’ he murmurs, looking at the pictures. The good news momentarily lifts the weary folds at the edge of his mouth but the smile does not reach his sad eyes.

‘Great,’ I say. I expected no less. I am 20 after all, and I will live forever.

‘But looks like you’ve started to grind your teeth. And you say the jaw hurts?’

‘Grind my teeth? I don’t think so.’ I run my tongue along the inside of my teeth.

‘Well, it happens when you’re asleep so you don’t notice.’

Yeah whatever pal.

‘Anything we can do about the jaw?’

‘Well, I can make you a splint. That’ll help both issues. It’s like a retainer that your front teeth rest on. It allows them to glide a few millimeters above the others so you don’t grind. And it will probably allow your jaw to relax.’

‘Is it hard to sleep with?’

‘Not really once you get used to it. I just made one for my daughter.’

Seems easy enough.

‘OK. Let’s do it.’

I’m 22, and living in Utah. The splint was great but I’ve lost it and I haven’t had a cleaning in two years. I looked up the top-rated dentist on Google and now I’m walking into my appointment.

I open the door and squint into the shining plasticky sleekness. ‘Hello and welcome!’ beams a beautiful girl with flowing blonde hair and red lips. She sits in a Herman Miller chair behind a white marble countertop. The lights are bright and fancy green wallpaper accents one wall. The office air is chilly, fancy chilly, the kind of chilly that says ‘we don’t care how much electricity costs, as long as you’re comfortable.’

‘Spa water?’

‘Oh wow, sure, thanks.’

The hygienist that does my cleaning is also beautiful, about my age. Ring on though…my sister was a hygienist for a while and wore a fake ring to keep the men at bay. 22 and married? This is Utah, so probably legit.

When did they start cutting scrubs to make them sexy?

Another girl takes my x-rays on a new machine the size of a small ottoman. She also wears form-fitting scrubs that somehow leave a lot and a little to the imagination at the same time.

Dentist comes in. She’s an attractive blond that paid for about 50% of her looks. She looks me full in the face and leans forward.

‘Good news. I can make you a new night guard. You said your last dentist made you a splint?’

‘Yes it worked really well. My jaw never felt better.’

‘Well splints aren’t good because your top teeth need your bottom teeth to strike against. Without that pressure they move around and eventually loosen and fall out.’

‘Oh jeez. Well, it felt great…’

‘I’m sure it did.’ She gives me a pitying smile. Her teeth are so white and her skin is so tan. If you smile while lying in a tanning bed does it bleach your teeth while it’s darkening your skin?

‘Now I have some bad news: you have twelve cavities.’

‘What!? Twelve cavities?’

I am shocked and embarrassed. I put my hand to my mouth. My oral hygiene isn’t that bad, is it? Jesus…I had no idea.

‘How could that be? Two years ago I had none. Do they grow that fast?’

‘They can!’ She brings up the x-ray on the sleek Dell x-ray viewer. ‘See the smudge between these teeth? That’s a cavity.’

I lean forward. ‘I don’t really see it…’

‘Well you can’t because you’re not a dentist. But I can. That’s the worst one. And you have eleven more.’

‘Oh gosh…’

I imagine great painful pits in my teeth, crumbling molars, my grandfather’s champing gums.

‘The good news is I can fill five of them today.’

‘Shoot, I would but I have to get back to work. I’ll reschedule.’

‘Well do it soon. There’s no cure for a cavity you know, and they’ll just get worse!’

Back at work I tell the guys the shocking news and urge them all to brush more often.

‘Wait,’ says Petey. ‘You said you went to Dr. Greene?’ Petey’s a quiet young Mormon guy, but now he gets heated.

‘That freaking dentist…she is the worst, the absolute worst. She said I had fifteen cavities! I was so darn scared. I had her fill the first few but she drilled too deep and I got an abscess and almost freaking died. Whatever you do, don’t go back to her. She’s just out to milk her patients. How do you think she affords that nice office?’

‘It was a nice office…’

‘Plus they give people discounts if they leave a 5-star review.’

‘Oh yeah…they had like 200 reviews and an exactly 5 star rating. That’s sketchy.’

‘Yeah man. Here’s the number to Dr. Frank, the dentist that fixed me.’

***

Dr. Frank’s office has a low drop ceiling with yellowing panels, peeling wallpaper, stacks of files along the back wall, busted-ass waiting room chairs. The fax machine is running loud and hot in the corner. The woman at the desk has normal, baggy scrubs. She calls me ‘hun’.

Dr. Frank is a wide man with a confident grip and a straightforward manner that lives up to his name.

‘I reviewed those x-rays from Dr. Greene. Let’s just say I’m not a fan of her work. She showed you these shadows right? Well I like to call that “trolling for dollars”. They may be cavities. They may not be. It will be years before we can say for sure.’

‘So I don’t have twelve cavities?’

‘Well some of them probably will turn into cavities some day. But not now. And some may just go away.’

‘Really? Because she said—’

‘Oh yeah, I’ve seen it happen. Look, if you were my kid I’d say don’t go drilling anything right now. Don’t let her scare you into doing something you don’t need to do.’

I’m 26, living in Burbank, California. Back in a dental chair with my mouth open. The place isn’t exactly dingy, but it isn’t exactly nice either. I’ve learned my lesson about nice offices. The waiting couch sags, the receptionist reminds me of my second-grade teacher and the hygienist has such muscular forearms that I wonder if she’s there to restrain patients as well as clean their teeth.

Dr. Hong is calling numbers out from inside my mouth to the hygienist who types them into a chunky old Lenovo laptop. Dr. Hong snaps off the yellowing overhead light and gives an exasperated sigh.

‘You need wear night guard. Your teeth terrible. Grinding and clenching all night.’

Damn it. I never got a new one.

‘Hahhyeah I han hegetha nother un hut eely herk?’

He takes the dam out of my mouth and hand-cranks the chair upright.

‘Yes night guard work. But only if you wear it.’

‘But—’

He waves me silent and drops his bombshell.

‘You have to wear night guard. You have teeth of 50-year-old!’

‘What?! The teeth of a 50-year-old!?’

I’m shocked and embarrassed. I run my tongue along the inside of my molars. I mean, I knew I should be wearing the night guard but, god… I had no idea I did such damage.

‘Oh yes, you have old teeth. Very terrible. But night guard only $250. I can take impressions for it today.’

‘But they’re hard to keep in all the time. And there’s my jaw...’

‘Too bad. You need to get used to it. If you my grandson I tell you wear it or you lose your teeth! And hurry up because I retire soon. I will refer you to TMJ guy for jaw.’

‘OK…let’s do it.’

I’m so cowed he could have charged me $1,000 and I still would have paid.

The night guard does not help my jaw. And it pushes a couple teeth out of line so now they strike wrong. Dr. Hong retired and I’m moving soon. I don’t have time to get it adjusted. Plus, is it really doing anything? I don’t think I’m really grinding. It was that stupid tooth reshaping when I was 17…

Eventually I get in with the TMJ specialist, and he refers me to an oral surgeon. ‘Best guy in town for a jaw like yours.’

It seems this surgeon is dental royalty because his dad founded the big university dental school. Junior is a hotshot surgeon but he’s retiring soon so I should get in with him as soon as I can.

I arrive at the swanky building off Wilshire Blvd. Elevator to the 30th floor. Doors open right into the office and I’m greeted by a bored, curvy little blonde with light brown eyes that flash up from her Apple laptop. She instantly catalogs me from under her elegant mascara. No ring. But it’s clear from the wince she passes off as a smile that I wouldn’t have a chance anyway. The office is nice in an old money sort of way: stiff leather chairs, thick wool carpet, muted red and white and gold, immaculately clean.

‘Spa water?’

‘Sure, thanks.’

Dentist is a large tanned man with a quarterback’s hands. He doesn’t use them to shake mine. He has pictures of dead African big game as his Macbook Pro screensaver. He touches his gold-rimmed glasses and pulls up my x-rays.

‘You have what we call a large skeletal anomaly. Essentially your face is deformed. The only way — the only way — to solve it is to saw your jaw apart, graft bone, cut off your gums and move the whole thing over fractions of a millimeter with posts and pins and glue made from your own powdered bone.’

A chill runs up my spine.

‘Plus you have some gum recession which we can take care of at the same time. It is a coordinated care plan that involves four different specialists. It takes about 9 months in total. It will cost about $100,000. Maybe $150,000. But I am confident we can probably help you.’

‘But what about—’

‘It is the only way. Nothing else is really worth getting into.’

‘But—’

‘Look, if you want things to keep getting worse, live your life. But if it was me, I’d bite the bullet and get it over with.’

‘In terms of a second opinion, I think his recommendation was way too drastic,’ says my neighborhood strip mall orthodontist. She’s in her early thirties, still paying off her student loans but not trying to pay them off tomorrow. Office is modest and her assistant is a niece with bad skin.

‘I guess there’s a skeletal anomaly but it’s not bad at all. About 6 months with some gentle Invisalign and you’d be all set. Your jaw will not be perfect, but I can promise that you’ll have a better bite.’

This should make me feel better. But all I feel is exasperation.

‘That’s great. But I don’t know what to think. I got him saying $150k and 9 months, and I got you telling me 6 months of light correction. Who do I believe?’

She shrugs. ‘Well, he’s a surgeon. Maybe every mouth looks like a nail he should hammer.’

I wince at the thought.

‘How could I have prevented this?’

‘Oh well you should have gotten braces when you were young. And a palate expander. But after about 21 your bones are hard and set. No changing them unless you do those crazy surgeries he was talking about.’

‘Damn. So just a little Invisalign?’

‘Yep.’

‘Would you need to do any tooth reshaping or anything like that afterwards?’

‘Oh sure. But that’s nothing. Just fractions of a millimeter. I can take your impressions today if you want to get started?’

‘No thanks. I need to think about it.’

I’m 33, just moved back home to Austin. I never got the Invisalign. Jaw still hurts from time to time. I haven’t had a cleaning in two years. And my tooth sensitivity from the gum recession is getting worse. I can’t drink cold water without pain. My teeth aren’t as sharp as they used to be either. I have not been wearing a night guard. Both my parents have recently gotten root canals and explained the process in graphic detail. They wish they had taken better care of their teeth.

It is time to get my shit together. But first I need to find a good dentist.

‘You should see mine,’ says my sister over tacos. ‘She’s cool and pretty. I call her Hottie Doc. It’s a super nice office.’

‘Hottie Doc? Nice office? No thank you.’

‘Oh trust me, I understand, but they really do good work and they don’t try to upsell you on shit all the time.’

She would know. She was a hygienist after all.

‘OK, well I don’t have any other recommendations and I don’t trust Google so… I guess I’ll give them a shot.’

Spa water. Beautiful hygienist. Cold office. New handheld x-ray machine. Form-fitting scrubs.

‘Well you have 6 cavities,’ says Hottie Doc. Her perfectly bronzed skin glows in the afternoon sun coming in through the floor to ceiling window. ‘See these shadows between the teeth?’

At least I see the shadows now, because they’re bigger. And those were some of the same teeth Dr. Greene said I had cavities in ten years ago. It’s time.

‘OK fine. And what about the gum recession?’

‘Yeah your recession is pretty bad. For that I’ll get you in with the periodontist. It's worth a consult and he’s great.’

‘And the jaw thing?’

‘Well you need a night guard for sure. I’ll make you something called a splint.’

‘Oh no, I’ve tried those before and another dentist said—’

‘Well, you’re not meant to wear them for a long time. A few weeks to allow your jaw to relax so we can see where it wants to go. Then we get you a proper night guard made in that shape, so all night your jaw is relaxed and happy. Your bite will feel off but in the morning it will just go back to where it normally does when you chew.’

‘OK, I guess that makes sense.’

‘And then we’ll refer you to the best ortho in town, Dr. Trudy. She’ll tell you what you need. Are you ready to take care of these cavities? I can do your left side today.’

‘Sure, better now than later right? But god I hate getting my teeth drilled! Every few years I read some promising article about how scientists are working on lab-grown organs and stuff. It’s always like 10 years away from actually being ready. When are we going to be able to just regrow teeth in the lab from our own stem cells or something?’

She guffaws. ‘I don’t know! Ask Elon Musk! OK now lean back and open your mouth.’

Poor form. A good dentist should have more professional curiosity than this. Further thoughts are drowned out by the scream of the dental drill.

On the way out the pretty little hygienist hands me two referrals. She seems too young for how much cleavage her scrubs are showing.

‘This one is for Dr. Trudy the ortho. She is just the best. That’s who my parents took me to.’ Her teeth are wide and white and straight. She has no skeletal anomaly. ‘And here is the referral to the periodontist Dr. Gupta.’

‘Thanks,’ I slur through Novocaine lips. ‘Guess I shouldn’t have been brushing so hard all these years.’

‘Oh that’s been totally disproven as a cause of recession,’ says Hottie Doc, appearing behind the counter. ‘It's caused by grinding and by genetics. Brush as hard as you want. I’ve seen gums grow back after wearing a good night guard.’

‘Oh really? I thought that once gum tissue was gone it was gone forever.’

She shrugs. ‘I’ve seen it. Bye bye now. See you next week for the other side!’

‘Yes, you have some light recession,’ says the periodontist Dr. Gupta. He pops in a mint and sits down onto a fancy swivel chair. Unlike other dentists, Dr. Gupta came by his dark complexion the old-fashioned way. His office is nice but I’m not sure if the same rule about niceness applies to a gum specialist.

‘It’s really not too bad. See all this tissue here? I’d say you’re fine.’

‘Well, that’s good to hear.’

‘The main thing is to manage the sensitivity and not brush too hard.’

‘Wait, I thought hard brushing was disproven?’

‘Not really. Who told you that?’

I feel a surge of anger. Good lord. Do any of these dentists actually know what they’re doing?

‘OK, well I’m getting this night guard which my dentist says will help with the recession.’ He gives a noncommittal head bobble. ‘I’m pretty excited about it because she’s making one that will help my jaw go back to where it wants to be.’

He frowns and squints at my jaw. ‘Hmm, yes. Look, just make sure it’s a flat one, and doesn’t pull your jaw out of alignment. Those sideways ones might feel good while you’re sleeping but then your teeth don’t fit together right. If it's off by fractions of a millimeter you could end up doing serious damage to your teeth and maybe worsening the recession.’

‘Oh. Well I already paid for it. I was really going to do it right this time…’

‘Well if I was your father, I’d say stay away from those types of night guards.’

‘Oh…’

‘As for the recession, if the sensitivity is really bothering you we can do a gum graft. That’s where I scrape tissue off the roof of your mouth, cut into your gums so they lift up in flaps, and then I paint the scraped tissue back on around your teeth and reattach your gums. It costs about $10,000.’

A shiver shoots up my spine.

‘Oh boy. Isn’t that just a stopgap though? Without really knowing what caused it, how do I know the recession won’t keep getting worse?’

‘We don’t. You know, if I were you, I would wait. We’re only a few years away from being able to culture gum tissue from your own stem cells and reapply it painlessly to your teeth.’

‘Really?! Now that’s what I like to hear! And who knows, maybe with light brushing and wearing the night guard, some of it will grow back on its own.’

Dr. Gupta scoffs. ‘That’s a myth. Once gum tissue is gone, it’s gone forever. Who told you that?’

‘My dentist…’

He chuckles. ‘Well, she’s not a perio.’

I catch the unmistakable odor of stale tobacco under the mint on his breath. I notice the outline of a pack of smokes in his scrubs pocket. For Christ’s sake, isn’t smoking a major cause of gum recession?

‘One last question. I saw Dr. Trudy for ortho before I came to you. If I do get the gum treatment, she said I should do the ortho first. Is that right?’

‘Oh, no no no! You do perio first and then the ortho. Moving your teeth around, even fractions of a millimeter without gum coverage, is a good way to lose even more. Listen, Dr. Trudy is…well, let’s just say I am not a fan of her work.’

‘You aren’t?’ I ask weakly. A gray swirl of frustration and confusion and hopelessness wells up inside me.

‘No. In fact, I’m glad she’s retiring. You know, I’ve seen a few cases like yours over the years.’

‘You have?’

‘Yes and with coordinated care, we could really correct your entire mouth. But the first thing you need to do is see an oral surgeon.’

He spins on the little chair and calls to the tall, raven-haired stunner at the front desk.

‘Hey Crystal, who was that really good oral surgeon out in California?’

blocks.x: I’m 17 and my jaw has been hurting, right at the hinge on the right side.

My mom has crowded teeth. My dad has gaps. I must have gotten a little of both because my teeth are straight and even. Good thing, because I’m in high school and braces would dissolve what small nuggets of game I have.
‘Well!’ declares the dentist as he emerges from my mouth. He pulls off his glove and I close my jaw. There’s a pop that could have come from either.

‘The thing is that the two halves of your face didn’t grow at the same rate. Here, take a look.’ He holds up a mirror and I see my disfiguration for the first time. The right side of my jaw is a little crooked. My nose on that side is angled, my eyelid is a slightly different shape.
‘Oh wow…’
I am shocked and embarrassed. I touch my face. I had no idea.
‘So, do I need braces?’

‘No, but your bite is a bit off. Fractions of a millimeter here and there.’ His own teeth strobe out from between his lips as he talks. They rival the overhead lamp for xenon brilliance, accentuated by his deeply tanned skin.
‘You’ll want to get it corrected or you could end up wearing your teeth down. I can do it today if you’re up for it?’
‘I’m not sure…what about my jaw?’
‘Oh it will make that better actually. Your jaw will slot right into place after this. No more sliding around to find the right bite.’
‘Are you sure? Because I really don’t—’
‘If you were my son, I would say the same thing.’
‘OK,’ I say, ‘Let’s do it.’

Tooth reshaping was a euphemism. Voluntary torture would have been more accurate. My teeth fit together better alright. But they are shorter now, and that makes the impingement of my jaw into the right socket worse.
Fucking guy. Never going there again. That hygienist was pretty though…mom-pretty, but still.
I wish I had never done it. But hey, at least I didn’t have to get braces.

I’m 20, in Florida. My face is still warm from the radiation bath the ancient x-ray machine gave me. It is a tall, forbidding machine that would have at least a dozen skulls painted on its nose cone if it was a fighter plane. The office is a couple rooms in an office building basement. The hygienist is out for a back surgery and the front desk lady is sick. So the sweaty old dentist is doing it all himself today.
‘Well no cavities,’ he murmurs, looking at the pictures. The good news momentarily lifts the weary folds at the edge of his mouth but the smile does not reach his sad eyes.
‘Great,’ I say. I expected no less. I am 20 after all, and I will live forever.
‘But looks like you’ve started to grind your teeth. And you say the jaw hurts?’
‘Grind my teeth? I don’t think so.’ I run my tongue along the inside of my teeth.
‘Well, it happens when you’re asleep so you don’t notice.’
Yeah whatever pal.

‘Spa water?’

Another girl takes my x-rays on a new machine the size of a small ottoman. She also wears form-fitting scrubs that somehow leave a lot and a little to the imagination at the same time.

‘Good news. I can make you a new night guard. You said your last dentist made you a splint?’
‘Yes it worked really well. My jaw never felt better.’
‘Well splints aren’t good because your top teeth need your bottom teeth to strike against. Without that pressure they move around and eventually loosen and fall out.’
‘Oh jeez. Well, it felt great…’
‘I’m sure it did.’ She gives me a pitying smile. Her teeth are so white and her skin is so tan. If you smile while lying in a tanning bed does it bleach your teeth while it’s darkening your skin?
‘Now I have some bad news: you have twelve cavities.’
‘What!? Twelve cavities?’

‘How could that be? Two years ago I had none. Do they grow that fast?’
‘They can!’ She brings up the x-ray on the sleek Dell x-ray viewer. ‘See the smudge between these teeth? That’s a cavity.’
I lean forward. ‘I don’t really see it…’

blocks.x: ‘Not really. Who told you that?’
I feel a surge of anger. Good lord. Do any of these dentists actually know what they’re doing?

‘OK, well I’m getting this night guard which my dentist says will help with the recession.’ He gives a noncommittal head bobble. ‘I’m pretty excited about it because she’s making one that will help my jaw go back to where it wants to be.’

He frowns and squints at my jaw. ‘Hmm, yes. Look, just make sure it’s a flat one, and doesn’t pull your jaw out of alignment. Those sideways ones might feel good while you’re sleeping but then your teeth don’t fit together right. If it's off by fractions of a millimeter you could end up doing serious damage to your teeth and maybe worsening the recession.’
‘Oh. Well I already paid for it. I was really going to do it right this time…’
‘Well if I was your father, I’d say stay away from those types of night guards.’
‘Oh…’

‘As for the recession, if the sensitivity is really bothering you we can do a gum graft. That’s where I scrape tissue off the roof of your mouth, cut into your gums so they lift up in flaps, and then I paint the scraped tissue back on around your teeth and reattach your gums. It costs about $10,000.’
A shiver shoots up my spine.
‘Oh boy. Isn’t that just a stopgap though? Without really knowing what caused it, how do I know the recession won’t keep getting worse?’
‘We don’t. You know, if I were you, I would wait. We’re only a few years away from being able to culture gum tissue from your own stem cells and reapply it painlessly to your teeth.’
‘Really?! Now that’s what I like to hear! And who knows, maybe with light brushing and wearing the night guard, some of it will grow back on its own.’
Dr. Gupta scoffs. ‘That’s a myth. Once gum tissue is gone, it’s gone forever. Who told you that?’
‘My dentist…’
He chuckles. ‘Well, she’s not a perio.’

I catch the unmistakable odor of stale tobacco under the mint on his breath. I notice the outline of a pack of smokes in his scrubs pocket. For Christ’s sake, isn’t smoking a major cause of gum recession?
‘One last question. I saw Dr. Trudy for ortho before I came to you. If I do get the gum treatment, she said I should do the ortho first. Is that right?’

‘Oh, no no no! You do perio first and then the ortho. Moving your teeth around, even fractions of a millimeter without gum coverage, is a good way to lose even more. Listen, Dr. Trudy is…well, let’s just say I am not a fan of her work.’
‘You aren’t?’ I ask weakly. A gray swirl of frustration and confusion and hopelessness wells up inside me.
‘No. In fact, I’m glad she’s retiring. You know, I’ve seen a few cases like yours over the years.’
‘You have?’
‘Yes and with coordinated care, we could really correct your entire mouth. But the first thing you need to do is see an oral surgeon.’
He spins on the little chair and calls to the tall, raven-haired stunner at the front desk.
‘Hey Crystal, who was that really good oral surgeon out in California?’

items.title: Americans' social activity has steeply declined in the past 30 years
items.author: hubraumhugo
items.summary: In recent years, there has been extensive discussion of a social decline in the United States, including a U.S. surgeon general advisory in 2023 that declared
items.text:
In recent years, there has been extensive discussion of a social decline in the United States, including a U.S. surgeon general advisory in 2023 that declared American loneliness to be an “epidemic.”

Various surveys have tracked America’s social decline over the past few decades. Tracking data from the American Time Use Survey shows that Americans are spending more time alone and less time with friends than they were two decades ago. Perhaps most notably, the American Perspectives Survey has found that from 1990 to 2021, the percentage of Americans with five or more close friends dropped by 25 points, from 63% to 38%.

But while extensive public tracking data show general declines in Americans’ socialization, little, if any, public data show what this looks like for the average American — how the day-to-day activities Americans participate in have changed over the past few decades.

In a new survey, Data for Progress surveyed 1,098 U.S. adults and asked them how many times they engaged in various specific social activities in the past 12 months. These questions directly replicate the DDB Needham Life Style surveys, which tracked Americans’ participation in various activities from 1975-1999 and were referenced in Robert Putnam’s 2000 book “Bowling Alone.” In this analysis, Data for Progress’ 2026 data is compared with the DDB Needham Life Style survey from 1995, which is the earliest year in which full data for all comparison questions was available.

This survey finds significant, double-digit declines in Americans’ participation in key social activities from 1995 to 2026.

The chart below compares the percentage of Americans who report participating in each tested activity at least one time in the past 12 months, between the 1995 and 2026 surveys. We find that Americans’ participation in various social activities has declined by double-digit margins, including attending a class or seminar (-22), entertaining people in your home (-21), attending church or a place of worship (-20), going on a picnic (-19), going to a club meeting (-19), playing cards (-19), going out to breakfast at a restaurant (-13), and doing volunteer work (-12).

A few activities have seen increased engagement: using the internet (+90), playing a home video game (+22), attending an exercise class (+14), going to a pop or rock concert (+13), and taking an airline trip for personal reasons (+5).

Methodology note: This analysis compares two surveys conducted using different methodologies, including differences in constructing sampling frames, modes, and weighting approaches. The findings below should be read as suggestive of trends, not a precise estimate of change. Please see the “Methodology” section below for more information.

One of the steepest declines in the survey is for “entertaining people in my home.” While in 1995, 88% of Americans reported entertaining others at home at least once in the past year, this number has declined to 67% in 2026.

Church attendance has dropped from 74% in 1995 to 54% in 2026.

The percentage of Americans who report having gone on a picnic in the past year has declined from 58% in 1995 to 39% in 2026.

There has also been a 19-point decline in attendance at club meetings, from 45% in 1995 to 26% in 2026.

This analysis adds to existing public data on America’s social decline. Previous reports have found that Americans are spending less time with others and reporting fewer close friends. This new analysis demonstrates that Americans are indeed spending less time in specific social settings, such as restaurants, churches, picnics, parties, bars, and social clubs.

Methodology

The DDB Needham survey was conducted by Market Facts using a stratified quota sampling procedure that begins with a sampling frame acquired from commercial list brokers. The sample oversamples by demographics such as race, gender, and marital status to oversample lower propensity respondents. Finally, the survey contacted individuals via mail.

In comparison, the Data for Progress adult sample was conducted through web panel suppliers and ensured national representativeness via quota fielding and post-stratification weighting.

There is plenty of research on the compositional differences that exist across survey collection modes, and this is likely to affect these results as questions about religiosity and loneliness tend to demonstrate modal differences and social desirability biases. We understand that these factors are at play in our comparison, but find that the magnitude and consistency in trends across measures is a substantial signal about trends in behaviors nonetheless.

items.title: We’re releasing Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for dreamers
items.author: emschwartz
items.summary: TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone
items.text:
TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone at your own risk. 🔥

Our philosophy

A huge debate we’ve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity.

To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally.

On the other hand, there’s no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We don’t want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers.

Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under “danger zone” flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases!

See these new capabilities as a continuation of what we’ve built over 2 years of stealth. They’re less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. They’re also an early glimpse into what we’re focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards.

Composable Images

Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, we’re enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love (jev-1.13.0) was multimodal all along!

Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets. You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state, instructions, or even criteria! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve.

As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot.

TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true

Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/images

Types Beyond Decisions

We’re introducing another new type as well: box. It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. It’s our first type that’s not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support.

We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so we’re enabling this only for jev-1.14.0 (spoilers).

Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/box

Size does matter, apparently 💅

We’ve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than we’ve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod.

We aren’t your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to:

TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true

Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length

Opt-in to help us

We love the community’s desire to help make models better! We’ve added an opt-in to allow you to help find model jaggedness with your queries. We will still not train on your queries, but this does make it easier for us to find issues and help debug your use cases.

jev-1.14.0

We’re also releasing a new version of Jev under jev-preview! Not meant to be flashy but instead be small, subtle improvements to everything. Most things should be a tiny bit better, but we expect the largest gain in multi-lingual support.

Model releases should generally also be strict improvements, but we’re well aware of how much developers hate updating their dependencies. jev-latest will be updated to jev-1.14.0 in a week. jev-1.13.0 will be available for a while.

We intend to give 60 days warning before jev-1.13.0 is formally deprecated, and 30 days for jev-1.14.0. We’ll release a deprecation policy prior to this.

Measuring Intelligence

As you all know, we dislike public benchmarks. However, we have our own internal best guesses on how to measure the form factor of intelligence that matters most for developers.

We’re trying something new out here: we’re going to treat you guys like adults and share this with you all.

Some nuance

This measurement is our best guess and will continue to evolve. If ever we show you our internal numbers again, don’t expect them to be consistent.

Don’t believe it entirely. Always favor your own experimentation and evals with your use cases.

We’re including only open weight models because we guard our validation set very closely and are spooked out about the data policies of our model providers.

This is likely biased towards our models. Feel free to ignore our model, and instead focus on the relative ranking of open source models.

What’s next

Lots of people love to ask what kind of sci-fi we’re releasing next. While we are working on some mindblowing stuff, expect most releases to be beautifully boring (like we think AI should be): small improvements across the board, better stability, and features for real deployment.

items.title: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse in Go 1.27
items.author: allddd
items.text:
Take a look at the following function:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
resp, err := http.Get(url)
if err != nil {
return 0, err
}
defer resp.Body.Close()
return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code.

Using HTTP/1 (GODEBUG=http2client=0), calling this function 100 times against
index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26
on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds.

That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference
possible?

The cost of establishing HTTP connections

To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make
an HTTP request.

Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and
HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS
endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:

TCP handshake (1 RTT): the client sends a SYN packet, the server
replies with SYN-ACK, and the client replies with ACK. Because the
client can send the first TLS message alongside that final ACK,
establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT).

TLS handshake (2 RTT): next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys
and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT.

HTTP request: with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent
after a total of 3 RTT.

These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly.
In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50
ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just
setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking
only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is
small.

Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be
expensive. Our opening benchmark queries
index.golang.org, which is distributed worldwide and
supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS
handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference
is still very noticeable.

Connection reuse

To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try
to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The
mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:

HTTP/1.0: while not part of the official specification, clients and
servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a Connection: keep-alive header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header
or sends a Connection: close header.

HTTP/1.1: connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for
subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by
sending a Connection: close header.

HTTP/2: multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single
TCP connection.

When connection reuse fails

In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the
same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two GET requests are
sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP
connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:

As shown in the diagram, net/http.Get reads and parses
the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate
net/http.Response, then returns immediately. The
response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the
caller reads from net/http.Response.Body.

Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream,
net/http can only find the start of the next response after
the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the
Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header).

Now look back at our example program, where we never read resp.Body:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
resp, err := http.Get(url)
if err != nil {
return 0, err
}
defer resp.Body.Close()
return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Through Go 1.26, when resp.Body.Close is called, net/http
sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse
the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections
for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing
new connections.

(HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames
over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an
unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing
the connection.)

Where failed connection reuse hurts

This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance
degradation in seemingly innocuous code.

As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s
status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that
provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"}. This will unfortunately cause connection
reuse to fail.

Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they
stop just short of the end of the body. For example,
encoding/json.Decoder stops reading as soon as
it sees the closing } of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response
terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still
unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is
consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though
it was only a single byte away from being reusable.

The manual solution

The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years,
many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is
done by draining the response body prior to closing it:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
resp, err := http.Get(url)
if err != nil {
return 0, err
}
drainAndCloseBody(resp.Body)
return resp.StatusCode, nil
}
func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
io.Copy(io.Discard, body) // Drain the response body before closing it.
body.Close()
}

While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing
a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of
the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to
drain:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
body.Close()
}

However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also
need to cap the time we spend draining:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
go func() {
io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
drainDone <- struct{}{}
}()
// Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
select {
case <-drainDone:
case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
// If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt the
// io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
}
body.Close()
}

Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a
response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background
and let it race against subsequent requests:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
go func() {
io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
drainDone <- struct{}{}
}()
go func() {
// Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
select {
case <-drainDone:
// If the drain can finish before a new request is sent, the
// connection will be reused; otherwise, a new connection is
// created, and the current connection will be put in a pool of
// idle connections, potentially being reused for another future
// request.
case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
// If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt
// the io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
}
body.Close()
}()
}

As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and
cumbersome. Worse, as the practice of draining response bodies spread, some
nuances were often lost. This has led to misunderstandings such as attempting to
drain response bodies for HTTP/2 connections, when doing so is unnecessary.

The current state and conclusion

Starting in Go 1.27, net/http.Transport
automatically does everything we have implemented in the code above: it will
asynchronously drain an unread HTTP/1 response body for up to 50 ms or 256 KB.
It also implements additional optimizations; for example, when a response
contains the Connection: close header, draining the body is guaranteed to be
wasted work, and it therefore skips doing so. Note that this behavior might
evolve in future versions of Go, as other possible enhancements become apparent.

As a general best practice, we now recommend that users simply close their HTTP
bodies once they no longer need them, like in our original example:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
resp, err := http.Get(url)
if err != nil {
return 0, err
}
defer resp.Body.Close()
return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Go is all about simplicity. Let your code stay clean and simple, and let
net/http deal with the complexities on your behalf.

blocks.x: Take a look at the following function:
It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code.

Using HTTP/1 (GODEBUG=http2client=0), calling this function 100 times against
index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26
on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds.

That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference
possible?
The cost of establishing HTTP connections

To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make
an HTTP request.

Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and
HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS
endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:

TCP handshake (1 RTT): the client sends a SYN packet, the server
replies with SYN-ACK, and the client replies with ACK. Because the
client can send the first TLS message alongside that final ACK,
establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT).

TLS handshake (2 RTT): next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys
and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT.

HTTP request: with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent
after a total of 3 RTT.

These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly.
In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50
ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just
setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking
only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is
small.

Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be
expensive. Our opening benchmark queries
index.golang.org, which is distributed worldwide and
supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS
handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference
is still very noticeable.
Connection reuse

To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try
to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The
mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:

HTTP/1.0: while not part of the official specification, clients and
servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a Connection: keep-alive header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header
or sends a Connection: close header.

HTTP/1.1: connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for
subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by
sending a Connection: close header.

HTTP/2: multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single
TCP connection.
When connection reuse fails

In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the
same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two GET requests are
sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP
connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:

As shown in the diagram, net/http.Get reads and parses
the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate
net/http.Response, then returns immediately. The
response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the
caller reads from net/http.Response.Body.

Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream,
net/http can only find the start of the next response after
the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the
Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header).
Now look back at our example program, where we never read resp.Body:

Through Go 1.26, when resp.Body.Close is called, net/http
sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse
the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections
for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing
new connections.

(HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames
over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an
unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing
the connection.)
Where failed connection reuse hurts

This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance
degradation in seemingly innocuous code.

As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s
status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that
provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"}. This will unfortunately cause connection
reuse to fail.

Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they
stop just short of the end of the body. For example,
encoding/json.Decoder stops reading as soon as
it sees the closing } of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response
terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still
unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is
consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though
it was only a single byte away from being reusable.
The manual solution

The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years,
many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is
done by draining the response body prior to closing it:

While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing
a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of
the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to
drain:

However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also
need to cap the time we spend draining:

Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a
response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background
and let it race against subsequent requests:

As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and

items.title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for fast on-device agents
items.author: gmays
items.summary: Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest
items.text:
Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally.

What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality.

Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion, which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization.

Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens.

Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads.

Post-training turns LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base into the agentic LFM2.5-24B-A2B in a five-stage pipeline as illustrated below: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), (2) Teacher Specialization, (3) non-agentic and (4) agentic Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and (5) Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL), training the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenCode.

During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.

This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments.

Benchmarks

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode.

The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength.

Fast inference everywhere

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem:

llama.cpp — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference

MLX — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon

vLLM — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput

SGLang — High-performance GPU serving framework

ONNX — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators

All runs were collected on Pipette, the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data.

Edge inference. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.
