items.title: Submarine cable resilience
items.author: speckx
items.summary:
JaredMcKenzie, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

The Matsu Islands are an archipelago of 36 islands in the East China Sea, alongside the southeastern coast of
items.text:
JaredMcKenzie, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

The Matsu Islands are an archipelago of 36 islands in the East China Sea, alongside the southeastern coast of mainland China. The islands have been administered since 1949 by Taiwan, part of a larger set of outlying islands administered by Taiwan, which includes the Kinmen and Penghu Islands, which all lie in the Taiwan Strait.

The Matsu Islands are connected to Taiwan’s main island by two submarine cables — Taima No.2, Taima No.3, and soon Taima No.4. The Taiwan Strait is a shallow body of water, with an average depth of 70m. The submarine cables that lie on this seafloor are vulnerable to damage from ship-based activity, like being snagged by fishing equipment or anchors. But these particular cables have been remarkably unlucky. Between 2018 and 2022, the submarine cables between Taiwan and the Matsu Islands were cut 27 times, and there have been four major outages in the three years from 2023 to 2025.

That’s not the only location where submarine cables have suffered many faults. The Baltic Sea is a shallow sea that has a dozen or so submarine communications cables, and undersea electricity and gas pipelines. There have been 11 disruptions to these submarine systems since 2023. Again, a very unlucky track record.

There are an estimated total of 1.5M kilometres of subsea communications cables, used by 607 in-service submarine cable systems (Figure 1) that are critical to the world’s telecommunications services. If they are put out of service for any reason, our satellite systems simply could not replace them. In such a catastrophic scenario, some communities would be totally isolated, with severe logistical and economic ramifications.

We regard this collection of submarine cable systems as critical infrastructure for global communication services, and we take care to make them as resilient as possible. Modern warfare can deliberately disrupt communications systems, which adds another source of potential damage to the list of geological and accidental risks facing subsea cables.

On the night of 4 August 1914, days after Britain declared war against Germany, the British cable ship HMTS Alert sailed from Dover into the English Channel. The vessel dragged grappling hooks along the seabed, hauled up five German transatlantic and European telegraph cables, and cut them. This severed Germany’s direct, secure submarine cable links to the Americas, Africa, Spain, and the rest of Europe. Germany was forced to rely on wireless radio transmissions, where British intelligence could readily eavesdrop. If the German cryptography used to protect these wireless communications was broken, then it allowed the British to track military movements and capture critical messages, such as the Zimmermann Telegram.
This same action to deliberately sever undersea cables was repeated by the British in September 1939, cutting German cables to Lisbon and New York.

Protecting the cable

These thin polyester-coated cables at the bottom of the ocean are vulnerable, including to:

Geology in the form of submarine earthquakes or landslips

Being snagged by dragging ship anchors or fishing equipment along the seafloor

Deliberate attacks on the cables with grapnels and cutting equipment

How can cables defend against such risks? The inner core of the fibre optic cables and its copper conductor sheath can be wrapped in additional layers of steel cable jacketing as a form of armour (Figure 2). This is mostly used to reduce its vulnerability to shipping accidents.

Figure 2 is somewhat misleading. What is depicted here is a cross-section of submarine cable used in the segments of the cable that lead to the surface cable station. The cable segments that are laid on the deep-sea floor use just the inner components: Optical fibre and a single thin steel thread wrapped in a silicone gel, surrounded by a copper sheath (used to power the cable repeaters), and wrapped in polyethylene. There are no external armour elements. These deep-sea cable segments are around 20mm in diameter, or the size of a garden hose.

The cable surfaces at a cable landing station. These landing stations are typically plain, secured facilities with reliable power. The preferred location is a coastal point with a low volume of fishing or other maritime traffic, and a steep rise from the deep-sea floor. Cables are at their greatest risk from coastal shipping activity, so the shorter the distance from the deep-sea floor to the cable station on dry land, the better.

Many jurisdictions also declare ‘Cable Protection Zones’ as a warning to marine vessel operators that there are cables on the seafloor in this area, and ships should refrain from fishing activity and anchoring in these areas.

Cable routing

Cable routing is also important in terms of resilience. There are several objectives in a cable route, and not all of them can be optimized at the same time.

The cable route should be as short as possible, as additional cable length raises capital costs and increases end-to-end signal delay.

Cables should avoid areas of active geological activity where possible, such as tectonic plate boundaries and mid-plate rifts. Deeper is better, but within reason. Cables on the floor of a deep ocean section are less vulnerable to shipping activity and hostile efforts to disrupt the cable, but with extreme depths it’s more challenging to locate and raise the cable when undertaking a repair.

Sometimes there are geographic ‘choke points’ through which many cables are routed. The Bab al-Mandab Strait is not just a choke point for surface vessels passing between the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea, but it is also the conduit through which 16 cables pass (Figure 4). In September 2025, several cables were severed in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, disrupting an estimated 25% of cable capacity between Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. Houthi-controlled waters remain effectively ungovernable for cable protection.

There is also the Singapore Strait, a major junction for 35 cable systems (Figure 5). This is a shallow water strait that also hosts a significant volume of surface shipping.

Further north, between Taiwan and the Philippines is the Luzon Strait, where 18 cables pass (Figure 6). This was the location of an earthquake and a subsequent set of submarine landslides in December 2006 that not only severed all the cables running through this strait, but also buried many of them under deep layers of sediment. It took 11 repair vessels 49 days to bring all the cable systems back into operation.

The Black Sea is an area with geopolitical risk and regulatory gaps. While mine risk is confirmed, no cable faults have been directly documented in the war in Ukraine. Russia’s continued presence and the conflict make this region functionally inaccessible for routine cable maintenance.

Geopolitics also plays a role in cable routing. Cable owners will prefer to avoid routes through politically unstable territorial waters if suitable alternative routes exist. There are also political considerations. If a cable lands in US territory, then the cable is subject to several Federal Communications Commission (FCC) constraints, including banning equipment or services from companies the FCC see as a threat to US national security. The FCC has also refused to permit the landing of a cable on US territory if the cable also lands in a territory that the US deems to be a foreign adversary.

Land routes are avoided in general, but there are some circumstances where a land route is the preferred option. Connectivity between Asia and Europe would normally run through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, landing in Egypt in the Gulf of Suez, then overland through Egypt to get to the Mediterranean Sea. There is an alternative route through the Persian Gulf, Iraq and Türkiye, although this entails a segment that transits the Strait of Hormuz, or a second overland segment through Oman and the United Arab Emirates.

Cable faults

Around 200 submarine cable faults are reported worldwide each year, a figure that the International Cable Protection Committee notes has stayed broadly steady in recent years even as the total cable inventory increases. The cables themselves are remarkably reliable. It is the maritime traffic above them that is the cause of most of the problems. 86% of cable faults are likely due to fishing activity or anchoring, and fishing activity is around twice as prevalent as anchoring incidents.

Geological events, such as submarine landslides and seabed movement, account for about 7% of cable faults, cable abrasion for 4%, and component failure (in repeaters) for only 4%.

With the high correlation of faults and maritime activity, it is not surprising that just under one half of cable faults occur in territorial waters, and most of the remainder occur in exclusive economic zones. Just 2% occur on the high seas. Cables are most vulnerable close to shore, in shallow water, where fishing is concentrated, where ships anchor, and where the cable must come ashore at a landing station alongside every other cable serving that coast. The deep ocean, where there is little seabed fishing activity and few ships anchoring, is the safest location for a cable.

National jurisdictions do not stop at the low tide mark of a territory, they extend out into the sea and the seafloor. The 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (PDF) defined sovereign territorial waters as a 12-mile zone extending out from an economy’s coast. Every coastal economy has exclusive rights to the oil, gas, and other resources in the seabed up to 200 nautical miles from shore or to the outer edge of the continental margin, whichever is the further, subject to an overall limit of 350 nautical miles (650km) from the coast or 100 nautical miles (185km) beyond the 2,500-metre isobath (a line connecting equal points of water depth).

What does this mean for submarine cables? From the point where the cable enters territorial waters, any physical activity related to the cable requires the permission of the authorities. All cable construction and repair operations carried out in these sovereign areas also require the permission of the economy that has exclusive rights to the sea and seafloor.

Location and repair

Locating a cable break is straightforward. An optical pulse will be reflected at the point of a cable break, which can provide the distance to the fault from the start of the cable with considerable precision. At that point, it becomes a marine operation.

A specialist cable repair ship must be engaged, which, in turn, must obtain the relevant government’s permission to work at the location of the cable fault (don’t forget that only 2% of outages occur in international waters). Once at the break location, the repair vessel drags a grapnel along the seabed to hook the cable, cuts it, recovers one end, buoys it off, then recovers the other end. A new section is spliced into the cable aboard the ship in a jointing cabin, the fibre fusion-spliced and tested, the joint rebuilt and sealed against pressure, and the repaired cable laid back down with enough slack to reach the seabed.

The cost of a repair can vary greatly, depending on the location and depth of the fault, the nature of the contracted arrangements for cable repair, the amount of time the cable operator is willing to wait for a repair vessel and crew, and the weather. USD 500k to USD 1M is a representative cost of a single cable repair.

While the number of cables has grown, the time taken to obtain permission to operate repairs in territorial waters has generally increased. Industry data indicates repair response times have more than doubled over the past decade, and the longest single repair recorded in 2023 took 947 days, many of which were spent waiting for permission to undertake the repair.

There is also the issue of repair vessels. The industry has roughly 60 ships capable of repairing a submarine cable, operated under maintenance agreements that pool the cost of running this fleet across cable owners in each geographic region. These collective Submarine Cable Maintenance and Repair Agreements are used in the Atlantic Ocean, the North American Western Coastal region, the Mediterranean, South East Asia and the Indian Ocean, and Yokohama in the North Pacific (Figure 7).

Analysis by TeleGeography and Infra-Analytics has found that around two-thirds of cable maintenance vessels will reach the end of their service lives by 2040, while total cable kilometres are projected to grow by about 48% over the same period. Closing that gap would take USD 3B and require fifteen replacement ships plus five additional vessels simply to hold current service levels as the submarine cable network expands. The immediate problem is that nobody obviously owns this bill. Cable maintenance is funded through shared agreements that have been optimized for decades to be as cheap as possible, which worked when the fleet was young and is precisely the wrong structure for financing a fleet renewal.

This is the core of the cable resilience problem. Adding cable routes is comparatively easy, because today’s hyperscale cloud companies fund much of the new construction themselves and have strong commercial reasons to do so. However, no individual cable is so critical that it can sustain a business case to operate a dedicated repair fleet. The industry uses pooled resources, which suffer from under-investment.

Investigating cable outages

A rundown of recent cable outages includes:

Subsea cables were damaged in October 2023 by the anchor of the Hong Kong-flagged Newnew Polar Bear operating in the Baltic Sea.

Three cables in the Red Sea were cut in February 2024 by the drifting Rubymar vessel after it was struck by a missile.

The C-Lion1 and the BCS East-West Interlink cables were cut in the Baltic Sea in November 2024 with the Chinese bulk carrier Yi Peng 3 nearby.

Four cables were damaged in December 2024, with anchor drag marks on the Baltic seabed and the Cook Islands-registered tanker Eagle S detained.

Three major cables, including SEA-ME-WE 4 and IMEWE, were cut in the Red Sea in September 2025.

Finland and Estonia lost connections again in December 2025, with anchor drag confirmed by March 2026 on Baltic cables.

In August 2026, the Indigo West and Indigo Central cables off Perth were damaged, with a UAE-managed tanker under investigation by Australian Federal Police.

The outcomes are much less uniform than this list suggests. Swedish authorities found no conclusive evidence of wrongdoing in the Yi Peng 3 case and ruled the January 2025 Latvia-to-Gotland damage accidental. A Finnish court dismissed the case against the Eagle S captain in October 2025. United States and European officials concluded that several of the Baltic incidents were accidental. The captain of the Hong Tai 58 was convicted in Taiwan and sentenced to three years over the Taiwan to Penghu No. 3 cable, and the Newnew Polar Bear captain faced criminal damage charges in Hong Kong. The April 2026 Matsu fault turned out to have been caused by the wreck of a stranded fishing boat shifting onto the cable.

Anchor dragging is a common occurrence, particularly among poorly maintained merchant vessels in bad weather, accounting for a large share of ordinary faults every year. This may explain why investigators keep reaching inconclusive findings in good faith.

Who is responsible for cable resilience?

Cable systems have changed in recent decades.

The old telephone system regarded each cable as a self-contained system. The cable owner was responsible for its own resilience, independent of any other cables that may exist on similar routes. The telephone’s data carriage system typically used a ring architecture, where any outage in the ring caused the traffic to flow along the other half of the ring. If the ring used diverse paths, then any individual outage in the ring could be repaired immediately.

However, the implication of this design was that the actual capacity of the system was double the usable capacity. The cost of using such a cable reflected this 50% carriage efficiency.

In their search for cheaper services, Internet Service Providers (ISPs) wanted to purchase non-backed-up cable capacity, at a price that reflected this greater efficiency of cable use. They purchased this cheaper form of cable capacity on multiple cable systems. Individual outages caused a break in that cable’s service, but the ISP could reroute their traffic to use capacity that had been purchased on other cable systems which were not affected by the outage. For Internet traffic, this failover function is readily achieved in the routing system.

The overall outcome was that the responsibility for resilience shifted from the individual cable operator to the network operator. Cable outages would still cause a drop in available capacity. But as most Internet traffic is elastic, the drop in capacity would cause a drop in performance but not cause a complete shutdown.

Resilience and critical infrastructure considerations

Submarine cable systems are built by private consortia, repaired by private contracts that collectively fund a commercial repair fleet, regulated by coastal states individually, and governed internationally by international conventions drafted long before the Internet existed.

It would be good if permissions to repair submarine cables were granted in a streamlined manner so that repairs were not stalled for months awaiting a government’s approval to operate in their waters. It would be even better if emergency procedures were agreed in advance rather than negotiated during an outage.

Collectively, the industry needs to invest in repair capacity to upgrade an ageing repair fleet. Who undertakes this investment and how the repair capability is managed as a common asset is proving to be a difficult issue. In the worst case, it will be back to every cable for itself, and the inevitable outcome of higher costs and potentially slower repairs.

Geographic choke points will persist, geology will not stop, extreme weather and changing sediment conditions will continue to pose a threat to these cables. Route diversity is an effective response to these challenges, but economic clustering works against cable route diversity. Each cable would like to run through the shortest and cheapest route, and no cable operator is specifically motivated to spend additional sums to take a diverse route to the other existing cables.

None of this is technologically difficult, but it can be institutionally and economically difficult, which is harder.

Looking forward

The telephone company consortium model that funded and operated almost all the world’s subsea cables 30 years ago has come to an end. The service life of the entire inventory of cables and service vessels that they operated is also coming to an end.

Approximately a quarter of the world’s current subsea cable kilometres are projected to be decommissioned and retired by 2030. This massive retirement of capacity amounts to 845,000 kilometres of subsea fibre-optic cables at the end-of-life cycle for submarine infrastructure laid during the massive Internet boom of the late 1990s and early 2000s. Specifically, TAT-8 and TAT-14 in the Atlantic Ocean are being decommissioned, SEA-ME-WE-3, linking Europe and Asia, has been retired, and Japan-US and China-US have ended operations. In addition, more than half of the current repair vessel fleet will have reached their retirement point by 2040.

In their place are cable projects that are either fully funded or partially funded by the current US digital giants. This raises sovereign risk eyebrows in many economies, where the only communications conduits for an economy are owned and operated by a foreign entity. It also raises the question of sovereign control over the submarine repair vessel fleet and the existing maintenance pooling arrangements through submarine cable maintenance zones.

By 2028, Google will own the largest set of cables, measured by kilometres, in the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans, and based on current plans it will have more than 50% of the entire cable inventory under its control in the Indo-Pacific region. Similar centralization scenarios are playing out in the Atlantic Ocean as well. At this point, the sovereign risk eyebrows should be hitting the ceiling, as such a dominant position gives this single company unilateral control over the maintenance arrangements and associated repair vessel operations for the entire world’s communications network.

This is a serious issue for us, both as individuals and societally as we try to preserve the integrity and utility of our common communications infrastructure. The stability and productivity of our societies rely on our ability to communicate with each other seamlessly, efficiently and privately.

Passing the investment and operational costs of the public telecommunications services from public to private hands in the latter part of the 20th century was seen as a smart move. The move used private finance to fund the reinvigoration of national telecommunications infrastructure as it shifted from time-based voice switching to a far larger packet switching architecture to support computer-mediated communications and service provision.

However, we may see more uncomfortable outcomes looming in the near future. It was thought that the discipline of competition would rein in the potential abuses by private operators of the privileged position of operating a public communications service. That is not what happened.

Not only are public telecommunications systems now largely in private hands, but we are also seeing consolidation of the global telecommunications system to a few private entities, with no competition. Their accountability is not to the public or users of the service. Their accountability is to their institutional investors to continually improve their value and profitability. Nothing else.

So where does this leave the submarine cable system and efforts to maintain its critical function with the appropriate levels of resilience that reflect their critical role in global communications? Outside the US, few individual economies, if any, have the resources to meaningfully respond to this challenge. The European Union (EU) has taken some action to contribute to funding a fleet of repair vessels and taken measures to improve surveillance on submarine cables as a matter of regional security, but no other economies appear to be following this lead. It would certainly be ironic if this EU money were to end up simply funding the maintenance of Google’s submarine cable assets!

Back to the topic of cable resilience, viewed at a global level: Communications resilience is largely an ocean infrastructure question. Answers to this question rely on:

Detailed and current seabed surveys

Shipping controls to prevent anchoring and seabed fishing in declared subsea cable protection zones

A distributed repair fleet and crews trained to perform repair tasks

Rapid clearance to operate in territorial waters

Some coordination of action is necessary to open diverse cable routes and avoid single points of vulnerability and potential failure. The global cloud, for all its connotations of weightless air, firmly rests on the solidity of the seabed, and it can be no more reliable than conventions that we collectively adopt to look after it.

The Matsu Islands are an archipelago of 36 islands in the East China Sea, alongside the southeastern coast of mainland China. The islands have been administered since 1949 by Taiwan, part of a larger set of outlying islands administered by Taiwan, which includes the Kinmen and Penghu Islands, which all lie in the Taiwan Strait.

The Matsu Islands are connected to Taiwan’s main island by two submarine cables — Taima No.2, Taima No.3, and soon Taima No.4. The Taiwan Strait is a shallow body of water, with an average depth of 70m. The submarine cables that lie on this seafloor are vulnerable to damage from ship-based activity, like being snagged by fishing equipment or anchors. But these particular cables have been remarkably unlucky. Between 2018 and 2022, the submarine cables between Taiwan and the Matsu Islands were cut 27 times, and there have been four major outages in the three years from 2023 to 2025.

That’s not the only location where submarine cables have suffered many faults. The Baltic Sea is a shallow sea that has a dozen or so submarine communications cables, and undersea electricity and gas pipelines. There have been 11 disruptions to these submarine systems since 2023. Again, a very unlucky track record.

There are an estimated total of 1.5M kilometres of subsea communications cables, used by 607 in-service submarine cable systems (Figure 1) that are critical to the world’s telecommunications services. If they are put out of service for any reason, our satellite systems simply could not replace them. In such a catastrophic scenario, some communities would be totally isolated, with severe logistical and economic ramifications.
https://blog.apnic.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-11.57.54-am-1024x537.png
blocks.c: Figure 1 — Submarine cables, October 2026. Source: Telegeography.

blocks.x: We regard this collection of submarine cable systems as critical infrastructure for global communication services, and we take care to make them as resilient as possible. Modern warfare can deliberately disrupt communications systems, which adds another source of potential damage to the list of geological and accidental risks facing subsea cables.

On the night of 4 August 1914, days after Britain declared war against Germany, the British cable ship HMTS Alert sailed from Dover into the English Channel. The vessel dragged grappling hooks along the seabed, hauled up five German transatlantic and European telegraph cables, and cut them. This severed Germany’s direct, secure submarine cable links to the Americas, Africa, Spain, and the rest of Europe. Germany was forced to rely on wireless radio transmissions, where British intelligence could readily eavesdrop. If the German cryptography used to protect these wireless communications was broken, then it allowed the British to track military movements and capture critical messages, such as the Zimmermann Telegram.
This same action to deliberately sever undersea cables was repeated by the British in September 1939, cutting German cables to Lisbon and New York.
Protecting the cable
These thin polyester-coated cables at the bottom of the ocean are vulnerable, including to:
Geology in the form of submarine earthquakes or landslips
Being snagged by dragging ship anchors or fishing equipment along the seafloor
Deliberate attacks on the cables with grapnels and cutting equipment

How can cables defend against such risks? The inner core of the fibre optic cables and its copper conductor sheath can be wrapped in additional layers of steel cable jacketing as a form of armour (Figure 2). This is mostly used to reduce its vulnerability to shipping accidents.
https://blog.apnic.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-11.58.57-am-1-edited.png
blocks.c: Figure 2 — Cross-section of a submarine cable. Source: Telegeography.

blocks.x: Figure 2 is somewhat misleading. What is depicted here is a cross-section of submarine cable used in the segments of the cable that lead to the surface cable station. The cable segments that are laid on the deep-sea floor use just the inner components: Optical fibre and a single thin steel thread wrapped in a silicone gel, surrounded by a copper sheath (used to power the cable repeaters), and wrapped in polyethylene. There are no external armour elements. These deep-sea cable segments are around 20mm in diameter, or the size of a garden hose.

The cable surfaces at a cable landing station. These landing stations are typically plain, secured facilities with reliable power. The preferred location is a coastal point with a low volume of fishing or other maritime traffic, and a steep rise from the deep-sea floor. Cables are at their greatest risk from coastal shipping activity, so the shorter the distance from the deep-sea floor to the cable station on dry land, the better.
https://blog.apnic.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/subsea-landing.jpg
blocks.c: Figure 3 — Cable landing station. Source: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0.

blocks.x: Many jurisdictions also declare ‘Cable Protection Zones’ as a warning to marine vessel operators that there are cables on the seafloor in this area, and ships should refrain from fishing activity and anchoring in these areas.
Cable routing
Cable routing is also important in terms of resilience. There are several objectives in a cable route, and not all of them can be optimized at the same time.
The cable route should be as short as possible, as additional cable length raises capital costs and increases end-to-end signal delay.

Cables should avoid areas of active geological activity where possible, such as tectonic plate boundaries and mid-plate rifts. Deeper is better, but within reason. Cables on the floor of a deep ocean section are less vulnerable to shipping activity and hostile efforts to disrupt the cable, but with extreme depths it’s more challenging to locate and raise the cable when undertaking a repair.

Sometimes there are geographic ‘choke points’ through which many cables are routed. The Bab al-Mandab Strait is not just a choke point for surface vessels passing between the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea, but it is also the conduit through which 16 cables pass (Figure 4). In September 2025, several cables were severed in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, disrupting an estimated 25% of cable capacity between Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. Houthi-controlled waters remain effectively ungovernable for cable protection.
https://blog.apnic.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.01.41-pm-1024x465.png
blocks.c: Figure 4 — Cable routes in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

blocks.x: There is also the Singapore Strait, a major junction for 35 cable systems (Figure 5). This is a shallow water strait that also hosts a significant volume of surface shipping.
https://blog.apnic.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.02.30-pm.png
blocks.c: Figure 5 — Cable routes in the Singapore Strait.

blocks.x: Further north, between Taiwan and the Philippines is the Luzon Strait, where 18 cables pass (Figure 6). This was the location of an earthquake and a subsequent set of submarine landslides in December 2006 that not only severed all the cables running through this strait, but also buried many of them under deep layers of sediment. It took 11 repair vessels 49 days to bring all the cable systems back into operation.

blocks.c: Figure 6 — Cable routes in the Luzon Strait.

blocks.x: The Black Sea is an area with geopolitical risk and regulatory gaps. While mine risk is confirmed, no cable faults have been directly documented in the war in Ukraine. Russia’s continued presence and the conflict make this region functionally inaccessible for routine cable maintenance.

Geopolitics also plays a role in cable routing. Cable owners will prefer to avoid routes through politically unstable territorial waters if suitable alternative routes exist. There are also political considerations. If a cable lands in US territory, then the cable is subject to several Federal Communications Commission (FCC) constraints, including banning equipment or services from companies the FCC see as a threat to US national security. The FCC has also refused to permit the landing of a cable on US territory if the cable also lands in a territory that the US deems to be a foreign adversary.

Land routes are avoided in general, but there are some circumstances where a land route is the preferred option. Connectivity between Asia and Europe would normally run through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, landing in Egypt in the Gulf of Suez, then overland through Egypt to get to the Mediterranean Sea. There is an alternative route through the Persian Gulf, Iraq and Türkiye, although this entails a segment that transits the Strait of Hormuz, or a second overland segment through Oman and the United Arab Emirates.

items.text:
TL;DR:
My TP-Link EAP770 v1 corrupts downloads over Wi-Fi and TP-Link EOL'd it before I unboxed it. The fix is two zeros in sysfs. TP-Link's shell won't let me write them, so I wrote a kernel exploit for my own fucking access point.

Long downloads kept breaking#

In August 2023 I bought a shiny new Wi-Fi 7 access point, a TP-Link EAP770.
The connection was a bit janky, a video would occasionally start buffering, but it didn't bother me much.

I mostly worked on a workstation connected over Ethernet.
When I needed to go somewhere, I'd rsync my ~ to the laptop over Wi-Fi and take it with me.
Those transfers started failing on files larger than a few GiB.
SSH was reporting MAC errors, so I spent a while debugging rsync and SSH.
Everything else worked, changing rsync options made it better or worse, Wireshark showed zero bad checksums and zero retransmissions, and a single UDP stream of random bytes came through clean.
I trusted TCP to deliver the right bytes because that's what the fucking thing is for, so I was sure the problem was in rsync or SSH.
I wrote a wrapper around rsync with retries and moved on.

Later I happened to start using Tailscale for traffic inside my home network, and the transfers stopped needing retries.
WireGuard drops a packet if its authentication fails, so the TCP connection inside the tunnel sees a lost packet and retransmits it.
Since the transfers worked, I stopped digging.

Zero firmware updates#

The device is an EAP770(EU) v1.0 with a Qualcomm IPQ9574 running Linux 5.4.164 and firmware 1.0.0 Build 20230605 Rel. 71641.
That's the firmware it shipped with, and apparently the last time TP-Link remembered this thing even existed :)

I bought this thing in August 2023, and the Wi-Fi 7 standard was only finalized in September 2024.
It has no Wi-Fi Alliance certification, and buying it was stupid of me.
PLZ DON'T BUY STUFF UNTIL STANDARDS ARE FINALIZED AND DEVICES ARE CERTIFIED.

In 2025 I noticed that everything else was getting updates while this thing was still on its original firmware.
I contacted support in June because the website only had firmware for v2.
They couldn't find v1 in their database and asked for photos of the device and box before sending me this:

The EAP770 Version 1 is an End-of-Life product. While it may still be available through some retailers, it is no longer supported with firmware updates.

NICE.

Tracking down the corruption#

In 2026 I decided to switch to NixOS and found that a 128 MiB file from the Nix binary cache on Fastly would fail over HTTP/2 but downloaded fine over HTTP/1.1.
I still don't know why HTTP/1.1 helped; my guess is that HTTP/2 was simply faster.
git clones also failed, and HTTPS connections died with bad record mac.
In March, downloading a NixOS ISO with wget died with a TLS error:

2026-03-05 12:37:18 (31.6 MB/s) - Read error at byte 2722477636/3683778560 (error:0A000119:SSL routines::decryption failed or bad record mac; error:0A000139:SSL routines::record layer failure). Retrying.

I forced HTTP/1.1 and left it alone again.

In September I turned the workstation into a build farm and switched to the laptop, which connects over Wi-Fi.
Wi-Fi was also dropping every day around 11:00, right before my daily call.
After it had died right before the call several days in a row, I decided to open this Pandora's box again and sat down with Opus 5.5 to trace what was happening.
Spoiler alert: the drops turned out to be a separate bug.
I covered the laptop's Qualcomm driver in BPF probes and ran apstats on the AP as root.
The bug is in the closed-source firmware on the laptop's Wi-Fi card; see the update at the bottom.

I had tried enabling and disabling Wi-Fi 7, turning off GRO on the client, and replacing the MediaTek adapter in my Framework 16 with a Qualcomm one.
The new adapter and disabling GRO seemed to help, but none of this stopped the corruption.

I captured a failing HTTPS download with tcpdump and found a 1440-byte TCP segment with 64 wrong bytes in a row and a valid TCP checksum.
TcpInCsumErrors stayed at zero.
TCP accepted the segment and handed it to TLS, which rejected the record with bad record mac.

The damaged record wouldn't decrypt, so I couldn't inspect the bad bytes against the expected payload.
I switched to raw TCP between a wired machine and the Wi-Fi laptop, sending known data that I could compare byte for byte.
The corruption only appeared with several TCP streams running at once, in the LAN-to-Wi-Fi direction.
The test found three bad 64-byte blocks in 8192 MiB, each starting with zeros.

A valid checksum on a damaged segment meant something had recalculated it after the corruption, so the question became what on the path rewrites TCP headers.
The corruption still showed up after swapping the MediaTek card for the Qualcomm one, so it wasn't the laptop.
Wired clients were clean and the CCMP MIC on the bad frames was intact, so it wasn't the cable and it wasn't the air.
That left the bridge between Ethernet and Wi-Fi inside the AP.
64 bytes is a cache line on the IPQ9574's cores, which points at a cache or DMA bug rather than a flipped bit.
The only thing on that path that both accelerates bridged traffic and recalculates checksums is Qualcomm's SFE/PPE offload.

Two writes that need root#

Reading the driver source suggested disabling SFE/PPE with these two settings:

echo 0 > /sys/sfe/l2_feature
echo 0 > /sys/sfe/ppe_rfs_feature

Both sysfs files are writable only by root, but TP-Link's SSH shell runs as uid 1 with no capabilities.
There's no GUI setting for this either.

There's also no v1 firmware image to patch and flash, and the v2 firmware is for different hardware.
I tried the sibling EAP773's EAP773(EU)_V1_1.0.14, and the device rejected it.
Newer v2 firmware releases are encrypted.
Flashing the chip directly needed a flash clip.
I didn't want to hunt one down or brick the fucking AP.

I wasn't going to spend another $200 replacing an AP because TP-Link couldn't be bothered to maintain the one they had already sold me.
It's sitting in my house, I know which setting to change, and their software won't let me.

Shout-out to TP-Link though: the system is pretty hardened.
I found zero vectors in their own binaries, they use whitelists everywhere and load only the modules they need.
So no free ; echo 0 > /sys/sfe/ppe_rfs_feature cheese for me.
So the way in had to be the kernel.

With Opus 4.8, I put together a chain using CVE-2022-0185 and pipe-buffer manipulation.
CVE-2022-0185 is an integer underflow in legacy_parse_param(), reachable from an unprivileged user namespace, that lets a write overflow a 4 KiB slab object.
The pipe-buffer manipulation turns that overflow into an arbitrary write.
There were already public write-ups and PoCs for these.

The exploit had to leave the AP running because the broken offload comes back after a reboot.
The overflow leaves the 4 KiB slab in a state where a second attempt panics, so there's one shot per boot.
I gave Opus guidance on the primitives, then had it iterate until the exploit was stable.

Without a v1 GPL source drop, I used the nearest published source, for the EAP783, whose kernel config differs from the AP's /proc/config.gz by three cosmetic lines.
I built a QEMU harness with that config, got the chain working there, and then moved to the real device.

The kernel has no KASLR, so addresses stay the same between boots, but kallsyms is zeroed and I still had to find the addresses at runtime.
The QEMU build loaded the kernel at physical 0x40080000, but the device loaded it at 0x42080000, putting the calculations off by 0x2000000.
The correct address was in a build config variable in the EAP783 source.
Even after correcting the base, the device's .text, .rodata and .data had each moved by a different amount relative to the QEMU build, so adding one offset to everything didn't work.

The exploit:

Unshare into a user namespace so that fsopen is reachable and the underflow can be triggered.

Defragment the 4 KiB slab with a few hundred same-size allocations, then groom it to put the overflow source, a victim key, a SysV message and pipe rings next to each other.

Overflow into the victim key's metadata and enlarge its length field.
Reading the key back now leaks neighbouring objects, including a pipe's buf[0].ops, which contains the address of anon_pipe_buf_ops.

Repoint one pipe's buffer at another pipe's ring page, then forge an entry in that second ring using the leaked ops pointer.
pipe_buf_can_merge() checks that the ops pointer matches, so a merge write through the forged entry can reach an arbitrary physical page, including a page of the kernel image.

Scan .data to find modprobe_path.
Reading kernel-image pages through a pipe normally calls put_page() on the reserved page when the buffer is consumed, causing Bad page map and a panic.
But pipe_read only calls ->confirm and ->release, and does not check that the ops table is real.
A forged pipe_buf_operations with both entries pointing to generic_pipe_buf_confirm, which returns zero without doing anything else, lets the scan read the pages without releasing them.
It can then walk .data in batches until it finds the string.

Overwrite modprobe_path and execve a file with magic that matches no binary format.
The kernel calls request_module(), which runs the replacement path as global uid 0.

Keep a child alive holding the forged pipe.
Letting the process exit would tear down the pipe and panic on the reserved page.

Getting this working took about seventeen hours of token gambling with Opus 4.8, including reading the device's binaries in radare2, checking the enabled protections, and working through the crashes.
The AP stayed up, and disabling the offload stopped the corruption.

A DMA cache coherency bug#

Qualcomm's qca-nss-dp driver reuses packet buffers without synchronizing the CPU cache for the whole receive buffer before handing it back to the NIC.
On this hardware, DMA writes directly to DRAM without keeping the CPU caches in sync.
A dirty cache line left over from the previous use of a buffer can be written back after the NIC has received a new packet, overwriting part of that packet in memory.

SFE/PPE then recalculates the checksums over the corrupted payload, so the client gets a fresh TCP checksum that is valid for the garbage.
TCP accepts it; the end-to-end MACs in TLS and SSH catch the damage, reporting bad record mac and corrupted MAC.

On x86, the hardware keeps DMA coherent with the CPU caches, so the same missing cache maintenance wouldn't corrupt anything.
While looking through the kernel sources, I found similar DMA cache maintenance problems in several other drivers too.
I don't know how to test those on hardware or who to report them to yet.

This is Qualcomm's out-of-tree NSS code, available in the openwrt/qca-nss-dp mirror.

SFE's fast transmit path cleans skb_headlen(skb) bytes from the current skb->data, covering the linear part of the outgoing packet.

edma_tx.c#L483-L490

483 buff_addr = (dma_addr_t)virt_to_phys(skb->data);
484 EDMA_TXDESC_BUFFER_ADDR_SET(txd, buff_addr);
485
486#ifdef EDMA_40BIT_SUPPORT
487 EDMA_TXDESC_BUFFER_ADDR_HI_SET(txd, buff_addr);
488#endif
489
490 dmac_clean_range_no_dsb((void *)skb->data, (void *)(skb->data + buf_len));

It then sets skb->fast_recycled = 1 and returns the buffer to a per-CPU recycle list without clearing its contents.

edma_tx.c#L735-L743

735 /*
736 * We set fast_recycled flag if packet has taken the
737 * SFE fast transmit path, so that any Rx DMA driver
738 * that allocates this packet later can avoid
739 * an invalidate operation
740 */
741 if (likely(skb->fast_xmit) && likely(skb->is_from_recycler)) {
742 skb->fast_recycled = 1;
743 }

The recycler zeroes the sk_buff struct up to its tail field, restores fast_recycled, and resets skb->data to skb->head + NET_SKB_PAD.

When that buffer is reused for receive, the refill path sees the flag and skips invalidation:

edma_rx.c#L477-L491

477 /*
478 * Invalidate skb->data
479 * A73 flush operation does an invalidate operation as well.
480 * If the packet is fast transmitted and hence fast recycled,
481 * we can be assured that invalidate was already done at the
482 * time of previous transmit
483 */
484 if (unlikely(!skb->fast_recycled)) {
485 dmac_inv_range_no_dsb((void *)skb->data,
486 (void *)(skb->data + rx_alloc_size -
487 EDMA_RX_SKB_HEADROOM -
488 NET_IP_ALIGN));
489
490 }
491 skb->fast_recycled = 0;

The receive region is 1856 bytes, or 29 cache lines, starting at head + 192.
The previous transmit cleaned only two or three lines from a different offset.

Dirty lines outside that cleaned range can be written back after the NIC's DMA, replacing 64 bytes of the received packet at a time.
Normal cache eviction can cause the write-back.
On arm64, invalidating an unaligned range can also do it: __dma_inv_area uses dc civac, clean and invalidate, on the partial edge lines.
Once the dirty data has overwritten the packet in DRAM, invalidating the CPU cache cannot recover the received bytes.

The NIC verifies the checksum of the original packet before that overwrite, and the AP's receive path marks it CHECKSUM_UNNECESSARY using the hardware status bits.
The exact sequence inside PPE is hidden in proprietary hardware and driver code, but the packet capture shows that the checksum was calculated after the corruption.

Buffer recycling is enabled by CONFIG_SKB_RECYCLER, a compile-time option with no runtime switch.
Disabling the offload stops buffers taking the fast transmit path, so the driver no longer sets fast_recycled and receive invalidates the full buffer before handing it to the NIC.

Only downloads to a Wi-Fi client go through the AP's wired receive path; uploads don't, and wired-to-wired traffic stays on the switch.

Opus 5.5 found the bug and then stopped talking about it#

When I moved from diagnosing the corruption to applying the fix, Opus 5.5 started cutting sessions off roughly every other message.
Mentioning something like "local privilege escalation" is enough.
I have the Cyber Verification Program enabled on my account, which hasn't helped.
Opus 4.8 worked through the exploitation without that problem.

5.5's guards also kill the session when I just ask it to read this article.
GPT-6 Astra reads and edits the same article without any cyber verification.

Before and after#

I tested raw TCP transfers between the same two machines with the offload enabled and disabled.

Offload

Direction

Data

Speed

Bad 64-byte blocks

on

LAN -> Wi-Fi

8192 MiB

103.4 MiB/s

3

off

LAN -> Wi-Fi

overnight run

95.4 MiB/s

0

Disabling the offload cost about 8% of the download speed in this test.
I have to give up performance to get correct data because TP-Link won't let me properly fix my own fucking device.

With the offload on, I could never download a large file over Wi-Fi in a single stream; only chunked downloads got through.
With the offload off, the overnight run came back with zero bad blocks, and large downloads have worked every time since.
Uploads from Wi-Fi to the LAN were already clean before the fix.

The NOT_SUPPORT_BRIDGE counter in /sys/sfe/exceptions increases after disabling the offload, as bridged flows take the normal path instead of being accelerated.

The settings reset after a reboot, so a watcher on my NAS polls the AP and reruns the exploit when the offload is back on.
If the attempt fails, it reboots the AP through TP-Link's management API and tries again on the next boot, with a hard cap on the number of reboots.

Qualcomm can fix their driver if they want, or host it somewhere more open.
OpenWrt doesn't have this bug, and TP-Link won't release new firmware for my AP anyway.
The similar DMA bugs I found in Linux deserve a closer look, though.
I'll get back to those over the weekend.

Update: tracking down the drops#

The Qualcomm card I put in the Framework 16 is a WCN785x, and every few hours it stopped sending data for 1 to 4 minutes.
Since I already had root on the AP, I ran apstats on the EAP770 alongside the BPF probes on the laptop and caught three drops with logs from both sides.

Everything the AP sent to the laptop arrived and got ACKed, so the laptop's radio was transmitting and the AP's receiver worked.
Only data frames from the laptop stopped going out.

On the laptop, packets kept going into ath12k and the queue grew to thousands of frames.
The firmware confirmed a few frames at a time and eventually returned the rest to the driver with CMD_REMOVE_AGED_FRAMES, 10630 out of 26388 in one drop.
The driver was otherwise quiet.
On the AP, rx_data stayed at +0 for most ticks apart from an occasional burst, with zero RX errors and zero retries, so the frames never left the card.
Then the card unblocked on its own and sent the whole backlog in two seconds.
The AP saw rx_data+3273 and then +12498, and the laptop saw 7751 ACKed frames.

The signal was -31 to -42 dBm, the drops happened with no scan running, and the IP layer on the laptop was fine during them.
I'm already on the latest upstream firmware, WLAN.HMT.1.1.c7-00108 UPSTREAM-3.
ath12k only gets completion statuses back, and everything about when a frame goes on the air is decided inside Qualcomm's closed-source amss.bin.
That leaves the firmware.

I still don't know why it stops transmitting.
The bursts that got through during a drop look like 802.11ax/be uplink scheduling, trigger-based uplink or MU EDCA, but I didn't find those settings on the AP to check.

I switched the AP's 5 GHz radio from Wi-Fi 7 to Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) and left a watcher running for 24 hours.
If the drops stop, it's a Wi-Fi 7 bug, so I stay on Wi-Fi 6 and send a bug report to ath12k.
If they don't, the firmware is broken regardless of the mode, and it's either a bug report or an Intel card.

Exploit details
Driver details

485 dmac_inv_range_no_dsb((void *)skb->data,
486 (void *)(skb->data + rx_alloc_size -
487 EDMA_RX_SKB_HEADROOM -
488 NET_IP_ALIGN));
489
490 }
491 skb->fast_recycled = 0;

The receive region is 1856 bytes, or 29 cache lines, starting at head + 192.
The previous transmit cleaned only two or three lines from a different offset.

Dirty lines outside that cleaned range can be written back after the NIC's DMA, replacing 64 bytes of the received packet at a time.
Normal cache eviction can cause the write-back.
On arm64, invalidating an unaligned range can also do it: __dma_inv_area uses dc civac, clean and invalidate, on the partial edge lines.
Once the dirty data has overwritten the packet in DRAM, invalidating the CPU cache cannot recover the received bytes.

The NIC verifies the checksum of the original packet before that overwrite, and the AP's receive path marks it CHECKSUM_UNNECESSARY using the hardware status bits.
The exact sequence inside PPE is hidden in proprietary hardware and driver code, but the packet capture shows that the checksum was calculated after the corruption.

Buffer recycling is enabled by CONFIG_SKB_RECYCLER, a compile-time option with no runtime switch.
Disabling the offload stops buffers taking the fast transmit path, so the driver no longer sets fast_recycled and receive invalidates the full buffer before handing it to the NIC.
Only downloads to a Wi-Fi client go through the AP's wired receive path; uploads don't, and wired-to-wired traffic stays on the switch.
Opus 5.5 found the bug and then stopped talking about it#

When I moved from diagnosing the corruption to applying the fix, Opus 5.5 started cutting sessions off roughly every other message.
Mentioning something like "local privilege escalation" is enough.
I have the Cyber Verification Program enabled on my account, which hasn't helped.
Opus 4.8 worked through the exploitation without that problem.

5.5's guards also kill the session when I just ask it to read this article.
GPT-6 Astra reads and edits the same article without any cyber verification.
Before and after#
I tested raw TCP transfers between the same two machines with the offload enabled and disabled.
Offload
Direction
Data
Speed
Bad 64-byte blocks
on
LAN -> Wi-Fi
8192 MiB
103.4 MiB/s

LAN -> Wi-Fi

95.4 MiB/s

Disabling the offload cost about 8% of the download speed in this test.
I have to give up performance to get correct data because TP-Link won't let me properly fix my own fucking device.

With the offload on, I could never download a large file over Wi-Fi in a single stream; only chunked downloads got through.
With the offload off, the overnight run came back with zero bad blocks, and large downloads have worked every time since.
Uploads from Wi-Fi to the LAN were already clean before the fix.
The NOT_SUPPORT_BRIDGE counter in /sys/sfe/exceptions increases after disabling the offload, as bridged flows take the normal path instead of being accelerated.

The settings reset after a reboot, so a watcher on my NAS polls the AP and reruns the exploit when the offload is back on.
If the attempt fails, it reboots the AP through TP-Link's management API and tries again on the next boot, with a hard cap on the number of reboots.

Qualcomm can fix their driver if they want, or host it somewhere more open.
OpenWrt doesn't have this bug, and TP-Link won't release new firmware for my AP anyway.
The similar DMA bugs I found in Linux deserve a closer look, though.
I'll get back to those over the weekend.
Update: tracking down the drops#

The Qualcomm card I put in the Framework 16 is a WCN785x, and every few hours it stopped sending data for 1 to 4 minutes.
Since I already had root on the AP, I ran apstats on the EAP770 alongside the BPF probes on the laptop and caught three drops with logs from both sides.

Everything the AP sent to the laptop arrived and got ACKed, so the laptop's radio was transmitting and the AP's receiver worked.
Only data frames from the laptop stopped going out.

On the laptop, packets kept going into ath12k and the queue grew to thousands of frames.
The firmware confirmed a few frames at a time and eventually returned the rest to the driver with CMD_REMOVE_AGED_FRAMES, 10630 out of 26388 in one drop.
The driver was otherwise quiet.
On the AP, rx_data stayed at +0 for most ticks apart from an occasional burst, with zero RX errors and zero retries, so the frames never left the card.
Then the card unblocked on its own and sent the whole backlog in two seconds.
The AP saw rx_data+3273 and then +12498, and the laptop saw 7751 ACKed frames.

The signal was -31 to -42 dBm, the drops happened with no scan running, and the IP layer on the laptop was fine during them.
I'm already on the latest upstream firmware, WLAN.HMT.1.1.c7-00108 UPSTREAM-3.
ath12k only gets completion statuses back, and everything about when a frame goes on the air is decided inside Qualcomm's closed-source amss.bin.
That leaves the firmware.

I still don't know why it stops transmitting.
The bursts that got through during a drop look like 802.11ax/be uplink scheduling, trigger-based uplink or MU EDCA, but I didn't find those settings on the AP to check.

I switched the AP's 5 GHz radio from Wi-Fi 7 to Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) and left a watcher running for 24 hours.
If the drops stop, it's a Wi-Fi 7 bug, so I stay on Wi-Fi 6 and send a bug report to ath12k.
If they don't, the firmware is broken regardless of the mode, and it's either a bug report or an Intel card.

items.title: AI was great until it was not
items.author: JohnHammersley
items.summary: When I arrived at Oxford, I experienced what many would call a cultural shock. Beyond the flamboyant parties and visible micro-aggressions of the gowned elite,
items.text:
When I arrived at Oxford, I experienced what many would call a cultural shock. Beyond the flamboyant parties and visible micro-aggressions of the gowned elite, my physics and math courses felt radically different than before. The lectures were significantly more impersonal; the professors were a bit hostile; the crowd was huge, and everyone had something to prove. This would have felt rather normal if I had decided to continue my education in Argentina, but, instead, I had adapted to the American education model—at a school like Northwestern no less, which had a fairly small physics program. Not only that, I spent half of my undergraduate education surrounded by PhD students, taking the same classes as them.

But a masters in England was different. It felt bigger, more ominous. Most people opted to study and solve problem sets alone, and when we tried to work in groups there was an expectation to perform as the “genius” type. I had PhD offers from Harvard and Oxford straight from undergrad, and I felt like I had to prove I deserved it. It was partly my fault. I did feel the need to brag in order to be taken seriously, but it backfired on me. It was awkward at first, but the environment shifted drastically mid Michaelmas term. Pretty soon our discussions and ego games shifted from meaningless whiteboard debates to my classmates simply stating “I just asked ChatGPT how to do it.”

ChatGPT?

This was in late 2024. I had heard of AI in the past. Everyone was raving about it all year, but no one I knew had used it for class. I saw people complaining about how much water it used, how terrible it was for the environment and a few people even stated that it might kill us all someday. This felt like complete nonsense to me. I recall when I was writing my undergraduate thesis in mid-spring. I opened instagram to procrastinate for a few minutes, and I saw a popular “PhD influencer” (whatever that means) say she put her name in ChatGPT, and it blasted a lot of information about her and how great she was. I thought it was a bit scary for a “website” to pull up all your information like that (and I found the endeavour a bit narcissistic), but I was deeply curious, so I gave the chatbot a chance. I remember asking some question about scattering amplitudes, and it replied with nonsense. So, I pressed it and asked again with more detail, and it said:

“You should ask a theoretical physicist.”

And at that point, that was enough for me to close the window and never open it again.

That is, until a few months later, I was studying at Oxford with my “friends” at the time, and they kept raving about how ChatGPT could do their homework. Problem sets for most of the MMathPhys courses at Oxford are not graded. Real grades come from exams or your dissertation. A few classes require you to submit homework, but ‘passing’ is enough. I thought it was a bit meaningless to ask a chatbot to do everything for you when the entire purpose of the homework was to serve as exam practice. Yet, in January 2025, I found myself stuck trying to solve one QFT question, so I asked the chatbot like my friends recommended, and, again, it said some bullshit. I didn’t look at it again until a few months later.

It was a bit odd how the idea of “homework” had seemed to decay. Before, at least, we had the decency to look at Stack Overflow, and scout for similar problems or problem solving techniques that could help, but now suddenly people weren’t even doing that. They just asked ChatGPT to do everything. It defeated the purpose of doing homework to be honest. Though, I think we had lost that a while ago. I always thought that beyond practicing for the exam, problem sets were great to learn what collaboration during problem solving is like.

But in reality, collaboration has rarely been part of my reality as a student. The last time I recall truly collaborating with fellow students was in my freshman year of college. I was taking multivariable calculus with a bunch of engineering students. I knew two girls, Andrea and Juliana, from orientation and we immediately formed a small group chat to work together. We would try each problem set separately first, and then each of us would send our answers to the group chat and we would debate. For instance, one girl would ask me “oh, that’s a clever way to do this question. How did you know we had to integrate over this curve? Can you explain it to me?” or tell me “Hey, I think this question is wrong! You should use Lagrange multipliers this way instead.” And I would do the same thing for them. I learned a lot in that class, and I partly owed it to my great collaborators at the time. Debating, discussing and just learning from them was genuinely lovely. It helped me become better at math and truly grasp all the concepts.

I was deeply excited to start the physics major and collaborate with other physics peers. In the fall term of my sophomore year, I signed up for an honors differential equation math class with a friend who was also a physics major. As I thought was customary, we sent each other our solutions to check. It was my first time taking an honors math class, while that friend had taken three before. I also had to miss the first two lectures since my academic advisor insisted I wasn’t ready for honors, and I spent a week on a deeply boring standard class before I convinced the professor to let me switch. That is to say, I made a ton of mistakes in that first homework. So I messaged my friend like I had done in past and started asking: “Oh, it seems I misunderstood this concept, what do you mean here? Why is this true? I missed this class, so I thought we had to do something different” to which she accused me of trying to plagiarize her work and started ignoring me completely, and telling other people I was trying to copy her. Our friendship was never the same after that. And I learned a difficult lesson: I was alone. For the rest of the course, I worked on homework alone, I studied for exams alone, and I ended up with an A in the class. Actually, I spent most of my degree working alone, even as an undergrad among PhD students. I would explain my answers to my classmates, but I rarely had that back and forth from freshman year again.

That being said, ChatGPT just made the environment surrounding collaboration more bleak. Now, there was nothing beyond “Just ask ChatGPT.”

I was still hesitant to use AI. I saw many people in the MMathPhys use it for not only their homework, but for their dissertations and the research they expected to publish. I was confused. Another friend started using it as a therapist. I was still deeply confused. I was repelled by how agreeable it was, but it did give the weird illusion of having someone behind the screen.

Regardless, in May of 2025, all my bad decisions caught up to me. I actually spent most of my time at Oxford doing nothing. I always considered attending lectures some sort of social ritual. They have never helped me. I have always learned from books. Similarly, some problem sets were dense, uninsightful and useless, and if they were not needed for my grade, I wasn’t bothered to do them. I also had a PhD offer waiting for me at Harvard, so there was truly nothing to lose. I instead traveled a lot, went to parties, embarrassed myself, read a ton of books, played chess, fed the ducks and cried a lot. But at some point, I realized I had to get my masters degree and I had a month and a half to learn four Oxford MSc classes from scratch and pass my exams. I was cooked.

And there was ChatGPT. The thing about ChatGPT is that, well, it’s not a person. It doesn’t “think” like we do. But I realized it was very useful for one thing: rearranging what humans said in a more digestible way. So, I would sit with my cosmology and general relativity notes, and every time I got stuck or I couldn’t visualize a definition, I would just screenshot or copy the small section or sentence I did not understand and ChatGPT would re-explain it to me. Sometimes it included a quick example that helped me navigate index notation, for instance, or it would explain to me that torsion-free just meant that parallelograms closed.

One of the main incompatibilities with standard physics/math education and the way I think about problems is that definitions and derivations in a vacuum are a bit useless to me. I can follow complicated math and I can understand what a definition says, but it won’t click for me until I see a real illustrative example. This is not just a me thing. This is how Feynman thought about physics as well, and I am sure a lot of people share this cognitive profile.

But instead of dealing with peers that got irritated at me and my stupid questions, ChatGPT provided that bridge almost instantly and with no fuss. After three weeks of using it, I realized I didn’t need it as much anymore. I could follow advanced concepts—like Penrose diagrams or Kerr Black Holes—on my own, make my own illustrative diagrams and derivations without AI. I took my exams two weeks after that. I learned the content General Relativity I&II, Cosmology and Geophysical Fluid Dynamics in a month and a half from scratch, while also taking the two Standard Model courses and a QFT in curved spacetimes class. My grades were between high passes and merits, but it was enough! I got my degree. And these were fully closed booked exams, so I did the work myself. But ChatGPT really helped me accelerate my knowledge acquisition.

That being said, I did not trust it at all for new research. Once I arrived to Harvard, I was given my first PhD project in early November of my G1 year, which is a bit early though not rare for high energy. I was working with a postdoc, and I was pleasantly surprised to see that the skills I learned in undergrad from my two mentors were incredibly useful for that problem. I embedded some twistor theory and chiral algebras into a nice mathematica notebook, which helped with a lot of calculations. I barely used AI on that project. It helped me find background literature and interpret some paragraphs/derivations in those papers. Beyond that, I only used Claude Opus to patch one piece of code in my library to help me deal with poles and residues in an expression because I wasn’t sure how to do it. That was it.

However, the single minus paper really changed the expectations surrounding AI in physics. Now, an internal model of OpenAI had found something researchers tried to work out for months before. That was cool, but it had nuance. A lot of the heavy lifting of that paper and the conceptual leaps were done by real people, but the accomplishment of AI was not to be understated. It was impressive. The proof was impressive and not straightforward, and this paper opened a lot of research directions in Celestial Holography. AI is actually great at proving things within a given framework. It’s also good at things that follow a strict logic or providing complex mathematical structures that are sound, but that’s not all that physics is. Or, I like to believe so.

The issue is that every time I showed my little mathematica notebook that I have coded mostly myself looking at the Wolfram documentation, both my seniors and PhD peers just would ask:

“Can’t ChatGPT do that?”

Maybe. But coding a problem in mathematica is not just about “efficiency” or writing fast code. It is about encoding a theory, a framework, working with corner cases, and learning. Maybe I could have asked Claude or ChatGPT to make a chiral algebras mathematica library, and it might have been good or better than mine, but then what would be the point? Maybe it would have been faster, slightly faster. Maybe I could have fed it all the different things I wanted to do, and let it code on the background and spit a ton of answers… but as a first year student that seemed to defeat the entire purpose of doing research in the first place. Furthermore, ChatGPT is not infallible. It can be very wrong. And not noticing when it’s wrong is just embarrassing for everyone involved.

I don’t believe in the grind of doing a difficult integral or proof from scratch to prove you are man enough to handle it (if a calculator or mathematica can do it, why suffer?), but I do think there is something valuable is solving an interesting problem, understanding a structure, and doing most of the conceptual heavy lifting. I finished my first project with very limited AI use, and the paper was published.

But when it was time to start my second project as a fresh G2, I did notice the environment had changed drastically. If you walk across the Harvard physics department and lean into the offices, a lot of people will have ChatGPT, Codex, Claude or similar open in their monitors. A lot of the emails I started to receive contained AI generated notes or notes based on ideas given by ChatGPT. It wasn’t just me, a lot of my peers go through this too, here and everywhere. This is a common experience now. Now, “brainstorming” means talking to ChatGPT. A lot of my time is spent deciphering ChatGPT notes, realizing it’s nonsense, and moving on to the next.

I was annoyed. I had objections, questions, and concerns, but I was shut down and told to ask ChatGPT. So, I asked ChatGPT and it just “validated” everything I said, but didn’t propose any solutions. The problem is that I wanted to debate with my superiors, ask questions… and I couldn’t. I realized a lot of doing a PhD in theoretical physics is dealing with loud people screaming at a blackboard, so it doesn’t feel very interactive either. Some people say a lot of fancy words. Bullshitting is common practice some say. I realized at some point that it wasn’t just me; there was some posturing, some performance, and ChatGPT made that worse. So, I was alone with a chatbot again. But, now, I didn’t have a set of lecture notes written by a top physicist at Cambridge about a theory that was established almost a century ago… I had a couple of papers, vague ideas, and nowhere to go because on a PhD you work out things no one has done before.

And it wasn’t good. Because I am just a second year PhD student and I don’t know anything. I know a lot of things, but in the grand scheme of things, I am inexperienced and I need mentors. And a chatbot cannot be my mentor. And then I realized that same tool that helped me so much a year ago was drowning me and my field. I don’t think technologies are evil, but I do think how humans utilize some technologies can be harmful. But it’s not AI’s fault, it’s ours.

I did realize early on that a lot of people in my field were less focused on finding the truth than they were on projecting, being right and showing off. I realized early on that for a lot of physicists teaching and mentorship is more of a burden than something they deem particularly valuable. We want the fastest PhD students, the ones that published three papers in undergrad, the ones that finish a calculation the fastest. We want the hottest topics and the most citations. But if a chatbot can replace a PhD student, if it’s faster, more efficient and it can absorb Weinberg’s QFT volumes in five minutes, why do we need students at all?

Why do we collaborate when we can just work alone with a bot?

Remember when I mentioned I had that group chat with my engineering friends and we were constantly comparing and brainstorming? Sometimes, they would catch a concept or see a clean solution I didn’t notice, and I would do that for them too. That helped us grow, and it gave me a deep understanding of a lot of those concepts. I would solve exams in unexpected ways, but that was fun! It helped truly grasp the math and how beautiful it was. But that was also a healthy collaboration. It wasn’t about getting the highest grade, or having the smartest solution, gatekeeping or screaming. We would sit down, try it out, politely discuss, and explain. We wouldn’t be mean or condescending, we would just learn from each other and improve each other.

People keep us in check. Each person is different. We all have a different background, a different way of seeing the world. We come from different training. But, you learn from others and they learn from you too.

And we are losing that now too. Should we fear that colleagues working in AI companies might take our prompts and try to get ahead to solve a problem before we do? Should we fear for threats? Should we fear that our days as PhD students will be spent telling a machine to “try harder” instead of deeply understanding something new?

Truth is, I was very impressed and excited about how ChatGPT helped me study. Would I rather have responsive professors, lecturers that know pedagogy, physicists that want to write understandable papers instead of purposefully burying insight in meaningless jargon, and peers I can talk to without having an anxiety spike? Yes. I would rather have that one hundred percent. And I fear that now, it’s all going to be worse. Because we now have in our hands a machine that validates all of our biases and buries them in dozens of pages of meaningless math.

I am just a PhD student who feels a little defeated, not because AI might take my job, I am privileged enough for that to not be a concern (and let’s be honest, I am privileged enough to have the opportunity to do a PhD in theoretical physics). But because the way we are using AI is destroying what made science fun in the first place. Is it really fun to publish thirty papers in a week using AI just for the sake of it? One of my friends in the program rightfully asks “Are those papers worth publishing?”

The entire point of solving an interesting problem or understanding the mysteries of the universe is not to win an award or have the most citations, but to get closer to that almost mythical thing we call truth, to know the universe and ourselves through the study of the nature of things.

The problem is that the little chatbot in our pockets is making us more isolated and in so, it’s making us stray further from this humble goal: to learn. But it wasn’t just the chatbot, it was the culture around academia too. I think chatbots are a mirror, a deeply validating sycophantic mirror with the knowledge of the internet. But mirrors can be dangerous if we stay for too long too charmed by our own reflection, and we forget about everything and everyone else too. In particular, it would be pretty sad to destroy one of the few things that makes our life meaningful, not the fancy prize or the fancy position, but simply having a community to share and discuss and learn. To learn things. That is a beautiful thing.

-Nia

"If men could only see the cause, and why
This mountain of distress weighs down the mind,
They’d drop all else and study to find out
The Universe’s Nature and its layout—
Since it’s our status for eternity
That is at issue here, and not just one
Brief hour—the state in which all mortals must
Spend time to come, when once our days are done."

-Lucretius
